#3760. London department store Selfridges launches sizeable GTA 6 takeover, featuring a varsity jacket that costs an eye-watering £2,500

Expensive British department store Selfridges has launched a sizeable Grand Theft Auto 6 takeover, completely making-over its Oxford Street London Corner Shop store and offering a considerable line of clothing, which includes an exclusive varsity jacket that costs a bank-melting £2,500. Note, you can buy the GTA 6 items online as well.

Live from Selfridges at Oxford Street for the #GTAVI activation🌴Rockstar are not messing around 🤯 pic.twitter.com/vqqXKwB1oJ

That GTA 6 varsity jacket is by far and away the most expensive item (and it's apparently already sold out), next to a non-exclusive varsity jacket that's £1,750, whereas the other items are pricey but conceivably affordable.

Quirky branded offerings include an ashtray, money clip and dartboard. It's all quite attractive stuff.

There's no word on how long the items will be stocked for or that the Selfridges Corner Shop takeover will run for, other than "while stocks last".

#3759. FC 27 Title Update 1.2.0 Patch Notes

Title Update 1.2.0 is coming to FC 27 on Nov. 10, and it includes major changes. EA Sports has already announced the highlights we can expect in this major patch, and there will be plenty of gameplay tweaks.

Let’s find out what to expect from the next major gameplay patch.

Gameplay is the main focus of this patch, and EA Sports has considered major community feedback.

Title Update v1.2.0 introduces our first gameplay adjustments for #FC27. Including changes to 95 Depth, fullback positioning, and more. Alongside key updates for Career Mode, FUT, and The Grounds.Read the full Pitch Notes here: https://t.co/QcjkIj9OgJ pic.twitter.com/DlkP0t4Asp

95 Depth will be nerfed, and the position of defenders will be adjusted. Unlike previous instances, they will now drop off sooner while still maintaining the higher line. This allows attackers to have more space to build their attacks.

Fullbacks used to drop deeper than intended when defending attacks. This has been adjusted, and fullbacks will now hold a firmer defensive line.

Similarly, attackers will do a better job at reading the opponent’s defensive line and make better runs to capitalize on the space.

The defensive line will hold a slightly higher position right after kick-off, making it easier to defend against opponents.

Auto-switching will be improved in loose ball scenarios, which also includes instances when a teammate performs a slide tackle, a headed pass, or when a shot misses the target.

Career Mode will also receive improvements in UI and other areas.

The patch will also feature plenty of minor fixes across multiple modes.

Hitmen are pretty common in the film landscape. They’re often the epitome of masculinity, secrecy, and, to some, sex appeal. We’re used to seeing hitmen depicted one way in movies, books, and TV shows. However, the idea of the typical hitman has evolved. Wild Horse Nine, which hits the 2026 movie schedule this weekend, may be one of the best representations of the evolution of the hitman.

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell star as Chris and Lee, two hitmen on one final adventure. It’s one of Malkovich’s best works and a film sure to gain a lot of award season attention. It’s a good film that thrives on its performances. The film also highlights that hitmen can have feelings.

Warning: Wild Horse Nine spoilers are ahead. Proceed with caution.

Wild Horse Nine is an impeccable bromance movie. It could rank among the best of this genre. Unlike writer and director Martin McDonagh’s Oscar-nominated The Banshees of Inisherin, this is very much a film about two men who still love each other. They’re not choosing to end their friendship; life is choosing for them. Lee and Chris aren’t overly emotional in the way people often characterize that trait. They don’t cry a lot in Wild Horse Nine.

However, they show their emotions in other ways, like being impulsive, irrational, and guided by love more than duty. That’s not often how hitmen are portrayed. They’re dedicated to their jobs and more emotionless. They make calculated decisions and avoid risky actions. That’s not Lee or Chris in Wild Horse Nine. McDonagh is a master at showcasing men as emotional creatures who act and behave like that, but in a very realistic way.

Men are humans. Humans are often emotional, even if they pretend to be steadier and more stable than they actually are.

Many of the best action movies (even lesser-known ones) focus on assassins or hitmen who live by a strict set of rules. This often includes not getting too close to anyone, because they cannot tell them about their profession. It would put this person’s life in danger. This is a common storyline that usually works well on film.

However, Wild Horse Nine showcases two men who have allowed themselves vulnerability. Chris even says in his recordings that he never really had a friend until Lee. I like the idea that hitmen live a lonely life, but they can sometimes let people in. It’s a risk, but most things in life are.

Chris and Lee are technically good at their jobs, especially Chris. He allegedly committed one of the most well-known assassinations in history. However, one of the signs of his deteriorating health is how bad he is becoming at assassinating. This is the comedy in Wild Horse Nine. However, even before Chris starts to lose his suave criminal behavior, I am not convinced these are top-level hitmen.

They make so many easily avoidable mistakes. Nonetheless, the movie wouldn’t be as fun if they were these flawless murderers. Wild Horse Nine showcases the marvel of being a flawed human, even with such a highly skilled profession. Wild Horse Nine is a must-watch fall movie.

I was fortunate enough to see an early screening of Wild Horse Nine at the 62nd Chicago International Film Festival. Catch it everywhere on November 6.

Spent most of my life in various parts of Illinois, including attending college in Evanston. I have been a life long lover of pop culture, especially television, turned that passion into writing about all things entertainment related. When I'm not writing about pop culture, I can be found channeling Gordon Ramsay by kicking people out the kitchen.

#3757. Super Smash Bros. Creator Masahiro Sakurai Cautions Against The Use Of Gen AI: ‘We Can Come Up With Better Ideas’

During an event celebrating 40 years of Japanese game magazine Famitsu, Super Smash Bros. supremo Masahiro Sakurai participated in a talk where he discussed his career and work. He shared his thoughts about generative AI, confirming that he has not yet used the technology for any of his current projects, and remains cautious over how useful the tool is in its current state.

The talk was held to coincide with the release of a new book in Japan compiling Sakuraiâs writings for Famitsu magazine. Over the course of the 18 years between 2003 and 2021, Sakurai wrote a column for Famitsu discussing the ever-evolving state of games development and his experience managing the shifting expectations and technologies within the industry. Alongside discussing his past work, the famed game director took some time to address many of the modern concerns facing the industry, including the growing debate surrounding generative AI. At least for now, Sakurai doesn’t think AI can handle tasks in games development or even the brainstorming process, and believes that âwe can come up with better ideas by thinking about them for ourselves.â

âThereâs more [to game development] than simply coming up with an idea,â Sakurai explained. âItâs not enough to just think up an idea. Lots of different factors come into consideration here, like whether you have a fixed deadline or if your team can do it, does it fit into your budget, and so on.â

Currently, Sakurai also believes the technology is not strong enough to even be used for brainstorming ideas, due to the need to factor in the realities of development and the limits on the sort of results it can come up with. He hasnât used it in any of his recent games, including the most recent Kirby Air Raiders, and currently has no plans to use it, doubtful of its capabilities.

That being said, he doesnât rule out its use entirely, as a result of the demands of players and the industry putting increased strain on the development pipeline. According to him, work on Kirby Air Riders was ten times more demanding than it was on the GameCube original, and he notes that there are examples of games unable to turn a profit even after selling millions of units. In order to bring down costs and make these games viable, he suggests the use of AI may be necessary in the future when the technology improves.

âIf you remain stuck on the idea of not using AI because itâs not trustworthy enough as a technology, thereâs a risk that you may fall further and further behind,â Sakurai ponders. âCompared to developers who make games without it, I believe those using AI without hesitation are likely to be able to create more games. As a result, not using may also be a bad idea.â

Developers from Shigeru Miyamoto to Kotaro Uchikoshi have shared varied opinions on the future use cases for AI within the Japanese games industry, and the broad adoption or regulation of AI by Japanese studios. As seen with developers like Sakurai, however, not all are willing to embrace the technology, or feel that generative AI is ready to be trusted with major development tasks.

#3756. "Art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI" Bandai Namco and Monolith Soft helped out with Ocarina of Time on Switch 2

Xenoblade series developer Monolith Soft and Bandai Namco Studios have been listed as support studios for the Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time, working on elements of the title such as "art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI". Special thanks to both companies appear in the credits for the newly-launched game (as you can see below) and a statement released by Bandai Namco Studios confirms its involvement, too.

"We were commissioned to produce some of the visual assets and artwork, including characters, environments, animations, cutscenes, and UI elements, for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a Nintendo Switch 2 game released by Nintendo Co., Ltd. on 5th November, 2026," reads a translated release from Bandai Namco Studio reads.

Of course, this isn't the first time we've seen Bandai Namco Studios' talents leveraged to help with Nintendo games: the publisher and its internal studios worked closely with Nintendo as a co-developer on the long-awaited Metroid Prime 4, and we know the studios are listed as co-developer for first-party Switch 2 titles like Mario Kart World and Splatoon Raiders. Typically, the work carried out by Bandai Namco comes from one of two dedicated internal studios that are contracted specifically to work with Nintendo: Studio 2 and Studio S. You can see a full list of the games Bandai Namco's support studios have worked on here. You'll note there are many Nintendo first-party titles listed here, going back to 2012 and Mario Kart 8. In late 2025, Nintendo acquired Bandai Namco Studios Singapore from the publisher, renaming the company Nintendo Studios Singapore.

"Alongside great judgement and clever tweaks, this astonishing remake has a proper ace up its sleeve," wrote our reviewer, Christian Donlan, in his five-star review of the Switch 2 game last week. "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

If - somehow! - you've already gobbled up most of the game and you're keen to play it again, you will be pleased to know that Master Quest code has been found in datamined files for the title, suggesting DLC may well be on the way in the not-too-distant future.

#3754. Hideo Kojima’s PHYSINT is somehow looking like a weirder Metal Gear Solid, and I’m all for it

Hideo Kojima and his PHYSINT project made headlines earlier this year when both moved from PlayStation to Xbox, but it’s still years off from releasing.

Kojima’s team is currently working horror title OD: Knock, but PHYSINT is on deck as an action-espionage title starring Bill Skarsgård as the main protagonist, plus Charlee Fraser, Dong Lee, and Godzilla Minus Zero’s Minami Hamabe. All accounts say it may be a spiritual successor to Kojima’s Metal Gear franchise, and new information only solidifies that.

PHYSINT at the Kojima Productions Beyond The Strand Exhibition! 👀 pic.twitter.com/UdRjXyKgbU

A special exhibit running for about a month in Tokyo to celebrate Kojima Productions’ 10th anniversary gave us a new look at concepts for PHYSINT, and yeah, welcome back, Metal Gear.

Along with an amazing sculpture of different appearances of Bill Skarsgård’s character, there are also two very distinct-looking mech designs, as shown in photos in the Twitter/X post above taken at the exhibit.

One looks like a Metal Gear, and there’s no other way to describe it: a bipedal tank with a sphere shape on one “arm” and what looks like a gun on the other. It looks like several other Metal Gear prototypes from MGS history, and something that easily could’ve appeared in the Konami franchise.

And then there’s the other one, which looks like a mech that comes equipped with three longer legs, akin to something like the alien ships seen in War of the Worlds with Tom Cruise. And at the bottom, a human man, showing the massive scale of the mech, towering well over the figure below it.

I’m all in, man. It just sucks that we’re so far off from seeing this title, but any sort of remnants of Metal Gear weirdness stuck in Kojima’s head with an actor like Skarsgård at the forefront? Sounds like gold to me, but we’re still several years from seeing it release, so hopefully OD can tide us over til then.

#3753. Skyrim lead designer hopes Sentinel will finally solve The Elder Scrolls' ladder problem

For such a simple, straightforward real-world object, ladders have been the bane of game developers' existence since the early days of the industry. And Bethesda's The Elder Scrolls Series is certainly no stranger to that struggle.

While we may be years away from the release of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, the recent title reveal reignited conversations about what longtime fans hope to see from it. That includes former Bethesda developers, such as Skyrim lead designer and Bethesda veteran Bruce Nesmith, who picked ladders as one thing he hopes Sentinel actually figures out.

If you're unfamiliar, ladders in Skyrim work in a weird way. You don't animatedly climb up and down them, but rather the character simply teleports from one end to the other. Speaking to The Examined Game (via GamesRadar+), Nesmith said that Skyrim's approach "really limits the art team in terms of how you can do multi-layer [levels]".

"It seems simple, it seems stupid, but you don't climb up and down ladders," said Nesmith. "All the ladders in Skyrim, you click on the ladder, poof, you're at the top or you have to climb a stair.

"But to do ladders, you have to deal with a whole host of questions which our programmers very legitimately put in front of us and said, 'You give me answers to these, I'll tell you how much programming time it's going to take to make them.' And you know, that caused problems right there."

Nesmith then pointed out the hidden complexity of creating functioning ladders in games, and the scenarios developers have to anticipate and account for, especially in a game as dynamic as an Elder Scrolls title.

"So, I'm halfway up a ladder, and [an] NPC decides to climb down it. What happens?" Nesmith posited. "The NPC has to have AI that will adjust for that. Does the player go through the NPC? Is he blocked by the NPC? Does the NPC stay on the ladder? Does the NPC go back up and know to wait and then come back down?

"And I'm just scratching the surface of some of the problems they brought up. So, it seems simple, and other games have climbing ladders, but we chose to put our efforts into other things to make them better rather than deal with that. So, I'd like to see Bethesda finally come around to making ladders a reality where you're actually climbing them and make the world feel a little more immersive."

While we know very little about Sentinel right now - much less how it's going to solve the ladder problem -that hasn't stopped fans from speculating about a number of topics, including what they believe is going to be a split / alternate timeline setup.

#3752. Sony Announces New Japan-Only PlayStation Portal With Internal Storage

Sony have announced a new Japan-only version of the Playstation Portal, with all-new functionality in the form of internal storage exclusive to the domestic edition of the device.

Last November, Sony released a Japan-only region-locked and language-locked edition of the PS5, reducing the price of this digital-only model from 73,000 ($461) to 55,000 yen ($347). In recent generations, thanks to the success of the Nintendo Switch in Japan and the high cost of PlayStation platforms compared to wages and the cost of living, Sonyâs once-dominant position has diminished. Sony’s Japan-only PS5 aped the decision by Nintendo to create a cheaper, region-specific Nintendo Switch 2. Now Sony is repeating this tactic for the new Japan-only PlayStation Portal, but this time the device appears to be an upgraded version of the hardware.

Although this new PlayStation Portal boasts the same 1080p LCD screen and general features as the worldwide iteration of the device, for this latest version Sony has added internal storage as an all-new feature. Oddly, however, it wonât yet say what it plans to do with this storage. Sony has only said that it “will confirm the future functionality at a later date.” Due to the addition of internal storage, the price of this Japan-only model will be identical to the global model at 39,980 yen ($252), and will be sold in Midnight Black, the same color variant as the Japan-only PS5.

The regular PlayStation Portal can only stream games, either directly from a PlayStation console or via the cloud. The lack of storage prevents games from being downloaded to the device, even though it has its own mobile chipset that, while different to PS5’s, would in theory be capable of running some games locally.

Does this new storage option mean that Sony will enable support for select titles to run natively? Will a similar device with internal storage also be sold internationally? Sony has yet to confirm anything at this time, but considering the success of Portal and the rumors of a next-generation portable, this certainly lends credence to the possibility of a hybrid approach. Pre-orders for the new Japan-only PlayStation Portal begin on Thursday, with a release date planned for December 10.

It won't be long before HBO's Harry Potter series hits the 2026 TV schedule and fans of various generations are introduced to a new take on the Wizarding World. So, this streaming schedule will see a whole new set of actors bringing their own doses of magic to the franchise's iconic characters. That includes Fred and George Weasley, and actors Oliver and James Phelps (who originated the roles in the films) have made a lovely gesture to their successors. And as a fan, I couldn't love this more!

For the highly anticipated Harry Potter TV show, Tristan and Gabriel Harland will be playing the troublesome but lovable Weasley Twins. James and Oliver Phelps recently spoke with TV Insider while promoting the latest season of their show, Wizards of Baking, and discussed the newcomers. Oliver revealed that after the Harlands were cast, he and James sent a personal message to Tristian and Gabriel:

We dropped them each an individual letter, just saying some experiences we’ve had over the years, and wishing them all the best with it. And it was a very, very, very private message or note, but it was more a case of wishing them all the best with what they’re doing, which I know that a few of the other cast members from the films have done as well.

I love that! When I hear that James and Oliver Phelps sent letters to the actors of the TV series, it reminds me of Harry getting his Hogwarts letter in the mail for the first time. As young Potter was given the opportunity of a lifetime through a letter, the Phelps' gesture somewhat mirrors that. On top of that, though, this is also just feels like a natural passing-of-the-torch moment.

Another reason I commend the Phelps Twins for reaching out to Tristan and Gabriel Harland is that instead of offering them advice, they simply chose to wish them the best in these iconic roles. Here's Oliver Phelps’ reasoning for that:

We just wish the best for those guys on their journey, because we were very lucky to have been able to play the characters for when we did.

Oliver and James Phelps truly are incredibly lucky to have had their Harry Potter experience, and they certainly seem to be cognizant of that. With all the new young actors taking over, I'm hopeful that their time playing these characters will be just as enjoyable as their predecessors'.

When the Phelps siblings previously weighed in on new actors portraying Fred and George, they said they wanted to give the new actors “their own space” to do their own interpretations. The British actors said, though, that they would always available for the new stars should they need help. It's great that the Phelps want the Harlands to have their own freedom to explore these roles, just like they themselves did in the movies.

So, wands up for Oliver and James Phelps for wishing the new Weasley Twins the best of luck. At this point, I'm all the more psyched to see how Tristan and Gabriel Harland will bring their own originality to the troublemaking twins we all love. (And I’m truly hoping the Phelps Twins’ TV series wish comes true, in that the Harland Brothers get to play out the Chamber of Secrets de-gnoming scene.)

Check out the new Harry Potter TV series when it premieres on HBO on Christmas Day and becomes available with an HBO Max subscription. The OG films are also available to stream on the same streamer. You can also find the Phelps Twins’ Wizards of Baking series streaming on that service, and new episodes air on Wednesday nights at 8/7c on Food Network.

#3750. Best WoW Forever classes

There's 9 Classes to choose from in WoW: Forever, and a lot of factors to consider.

The nine Classes of World of Warcraft: Forever are the same ones vanilla launched with in 2004, and they look nothing like what we have in Retail more than 20 years later. But Forever reimagines the vanilla experience, and Blizzard wants to “upgrade” how the Classes feel this time around.

The goal is for Classes to feel as balanced as possible without ruining how interesting their playstyles are, so Forever had a starting roster that felt rather nostalgic but still new enough to be unpredictable. But since Classes are made to feel and play differently from each other, you’d eventually be drawn to certain Classes for specific playstyles.

All Classes in Forever have something to offer, and they’re all versatile enough to offer more than two playstyles (through Specializations) even if they seem to be locked to a specific role. Staples you’re likely familiar with include:

Some Classes also provide some variety due to their mechanics:

Gold is not an easy currency to acquire in your Forever experience, especially as you level up (sometimes even with an alt!). Before you get your first Gold piece, you need to get through your Coppers and Silvers first. And with some of the game’s best gear, consumables, and materials locked behind a lot of Gold, you’d want to get as much Gold as fast as possible.

In principle, here’s how you often farm Gold in Forever, and this extends to the core World of Warcraft experience:

Among the Classes, here are standouts when it comes to Gold farming:

Of the rulesets in Forever, you might find yourself gravitating towards the Normal or PvE experience first. This is where most standard-fare open-world adventuring, and where raids and dungeons attract the most number of players. Besides Level 60, getting geared up for these PvE experiences is part of your capstones as you reach the higher levels.

There’s always room for pretty much any Class in a PvE party, but you might find some Classes preferred over others due to their inherent capabilities. Here’s a quick breakdown of where Classes usually fit in a PvE group:

You’d sometimes want a Class that is the best at something, but there are Classes with specs versatile enough to let them adjust combat strategies on the fly. These are hybrid roles, and some Classes excel at them:

Compared to hybrid roles, damage in PvE is allocated to Classes whose sole focus is to dish out as much DPS as possible. They are often glass cannons in that respect, so it’s the job of hybrid roles to make sure they remain alive long enough to actually kill mobs and demolish bosses.

Mages and Warlocks remain the strongest in the DPS caster categories, and your party can’t go wrong with either:

The same goes for Rogues and Hunters, but for melee DPS:

There’s no use working hard to fight in a dungeon when you’re dead as soon as the boss dishes out its AOE. And this is also the reason why the pressure’s on for healers to do their work properly, as it’s painfully obvious when the healers aren’t pulling the numbers they need since everyone else runs away to heal on their own. That, or a party wipe.

Thankfully, if you’re looking to train as a healer, you only really have four Classes you can focus on:

If you want to sink your teeth into PvP in Forever, you might notice that you’re getting into not one playstyle but actually three different types of mechanics. When you turn on your World PvP, anyone from another faction can fight you wherever, so if you can’t handle surprises, then you’re a goner.

Alternatively, there are PvP matches you can prepare for. Battlegrounds are faction-based matchups on instanced maps with point-based mechanics. Then there are duels, which are pretty much arranged fights between you and someone else.

The suggestions below will be based on what we can theorycraft with the Talent Trees, and what can be observed with Level 1 to 30 fights. Until we get to the real endgame in a couple of weeks, we can’t be 100% sure.

World PvP happens in the open, so the most ideal PvP Classes to take on enemies in the wild are the ones equipped for surprises.

Marksmanship/Survival Hunters specialize in long-range ambushes, which means they can run if they feel like they’re overwhelmed. With Track Humanoids on the map, they can set up slows and traps so targets never reliably reach them. And with Dismember, Sonic Blast, and Viper Sting in the mix, Hunters can pick targets easily… assuming they strike first. If Hunters are jumped on, they hardly have any way to disengage.

Druids and Rogues use the same formula here, in that they strike from the shadows and overwhelm enemies to submission:

The Frost Mage is interesting, as they’re only as devastating as the movement debuffs they can dish out. In theory, a Mage controls PvP with freezes and slows, then finishes with Ice Lance and Frostbolt. But if a target knows their mobility, the Mage can find it difficult to keep up.

Suppose you want the kind of PvP where someone invites you to a fight, and you duke it out fair and square, tournament-style. That means the Classes to choose are ideally built to target just one threat and defend against attacks that target only you. In that case, great Class picks would be:

Depending on the map, Battlegrounds are either capture the flag (Warsong Gulch), resource races (Arathi Basin, Darkspear Islands), or large-scale battles (Alterac Valley). Their objectives might differ, but the setup is the same – you’re all part of a team. This means the best Classes are both team players and built to kill:

#3749. Nintendo's legendary Kirby designer Masahiro Sakurai weighs in on gen-AI, saying "it has yet to gain my trust" but not to reject it completely

"Doing nothing is probably not the right approach."

Masahiro Sakurai, the designer behind many iconic Nintendo franchises such as Super Smash Bros. and several Kirby titles, has weighed in on the ongoing discussion of generative-AI use in game development.

At an event celebrating the release of his new book - Masahiro Sakurai’s Thoughts on Games - the veteran director told Famitsu he hasn't and currently isn't using the technology to make games, noting that the role of a designer is to generate ideas.

"It has yet to gain my trust," Sakurai said via DeepL machine translation. Regarding graphical use specifically, he added that, "It must not amount to exploitation of any kind," and that "for the time being, we can produce better results by coming up with ideas ourselves".

But Sakurai is wary of rejecting gen-AI completely, saying "making games today is far too difficult", with some games "running at a loss even after selling millions of copies". A company in that position may go under if it does not change its stance on generative-AI, he suggested. "Doing nothing is probably not the right approach," he said, but "where and how to use it" is a complex topic with a lot of uncertainties. Sakurai is taking "a slow-paced approach" for now.

Outside of regular industry layoffs, the use of generative-AI in games has been the most controversial topic amongst developers and players. Some argue it's already being used in multiple development disciplines, notably programming and writing code. Others, such as Shigeru Miyamoto, are more sceptical of the technology's capabilities, especially when it comes to the more creative and art-driven parts of game development.

You've got to hand it to floppy disks. The now 55-year-old storage tech occasionally crops up in the most surprising of places, like a San Francisco light rail line or, previously, US nuclear launch facilities.

One last holdout appears to be the Federal Aviation Administration, which still uses the disks for data storage within the US air traffic control system (via Ars Technica). Not for much longer, it seems, as US transportation secretary Sean P. Duffy has announced the widespread rollout of their long-overdue replacement.

"Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in," says Duffy in an FAA press release. "The greatest nation in the world deserves a state-of-the-art air traffic control system, and under President Trump, we’re delivering just that."

The ageing disks contain "vital weather and other critical information" used within the current air traffic control system, but that's set to change with the new Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS).

"E-IDS gives air traffic controllers the information they need to make timely decisions and keep the flying public safe,” says FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford.

"We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports across the National Airspace System."

E-IDS aims to improve the collection of pilot reports (referred to as PIREPS) and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs), with the former representing first-hand reports on weather conditions from pilots to air traffic controllers, and vice versa.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

One of the systems being replaced is called the Information Display System 4 (IDS-4), which appears to rely on floppy drive-equipped machines running MS-DOS. The FAA plans to complete the upgrade to the new system at 435 sites by the end of 2028, with Atlantic City International Airport and Nashville International Airport being some of the first locations to receive the new system.

Here's hoping the upgrade process goes smoothly, not least because I travel through US airspace on the regular. For giggles, I used this calculator to work out how many 3.5-inch, 1.44 MB floppy disks would be needed to contain the 30 GB base client of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

It's 20,834. With fun facts like that up my sleeve, don't you wish you were sitting next to me on your next flight?

#3746. Activision cracking down on popular Call of Duty: Warzone app that basically constituted cheating

"Lobby shopping" is what Call of Duty: Warzone players have been calling the ability to check the skill level of players in a lobby prior to joining it, enabling them to pass on those that include a lot of tough competition.

There are several ways players, notably Twitch streamers and content creators, have been able to do that over the years. But the use of one app in particular - Warzone Agent - has been considered by many to be cheating, and Activision is finally doing something about it.

Alongside the launch of Modern Warfare 4's version of Warzone and the game's first season of post-launch content, Call of Duty's anti-cheat team Ricochet has announced it's officially cracking down on Warzone Agent.

"Yesterday, we began taking action against Warzone Agent, a paid, unauthorised third party tool that lets users lobby shop in Warzone," the developer revealed in a post on X. "Ricochet anti-cheat will block players attempting to load the software and instruct them to unload it before accessing multiplayer."

Having the ability to cherrypick the lobby with the lowest-skilled players possible bypasses the game's matchmaking algorithm, potentially ruining the game for the dozens of other players in the match. Historically, content creators have used the app (and other methods) to post impressive kill records.

The developer added in a follow-up message that: "Using unauthorised software to manipulate the player experience violates Activision terms of use and leaves your account and hardware subject to enforcement." The language seems to stop just short of outright confirming those players using Warzone Agent will be banned.

As part of this crackdown, Ricochet reiterated its stance on boosting - artificially increasing (or decreasing) one's skill rating - saying that it too is considered cheating. "Receiving a boost, having another player log in to boost your account, or purchasing a boosted account are all against policy," the developer said.

"Boosting services flood lobbies with low effort accounts used to farm XP and complete challenges. Those accounts can later be sold as Ranked Play ready, directly feeding the cheating marketplace."

More than 20,000 boosting-related accounts have been removed since the launch of Modern Warfare 4, according to the developer, and Ricochet will "continue to apply pressure" in this area.

The quality of multiplayer was a particular highlight in Eurogamer's review of Modern Warfare 4, in which Dom Peppiatt lauded the complexity of weapon handling, which works without taking away from accessibility of the gunplay.

Another weekend means a new set of movies have hit theaters, and a particularly big title made its debut this week. The highly anticipated Godzilla Minus Zero hit cinemas, and it reigned supreme at the box office this weekend. Not only that, but the film set a major milestone in the process. I thought well-reviewed the glowing Minus Zero reviews might help the movie's chances, but I'd be lying if I said I thought it would earn a monster-sized achievement.

The sequel to 2023's Godzilla Minus One, this latest film from director Takashi Yamazaki earned $31,610,000 in its first three days. And, as a result of that, it now holds the all-time record for biggest opening weekend for a foreign live-action film. If anything, Minus Zero proved that shifting the Godzilla IP into weirder territory was the right move. It handily beat out The Cat In The Hat, despite the family-friendly movie's $20,500,000 being above what it was predicted to do by a few million. Check out the full rundown of the weekend below:

In man ways, it's not shocking to Godzilla Minus Zero do so well, given the acclaim the first movie received. However, I still wasn't expecting it to make box office history in such a way. Nevertheless, this weekend, it's the biggest IP out of the group above, and the biggest number-one take in a weekend since Street Fighter first hit the box office. I'm eager to see how it does next week and how it'll hang around the top ten list.

Godzilla Minus Zero Director’s Take On How He’s Adding ‘Terror’ To The Film Has Me Pumped

In other noteworthy news, You Can See Everything dropped from its top spot in the previous week to fourth place. Despite that significant change in the standings, the much-discussed documentary only brought in about two million less than the previous week. The fact it only brought in $675,000 less than Clayface could suggest continued business.

Wicker, meanwhile, continues to hold strong with a not-so-substantial decline from the previous week. Given there's a strong release lineup set for the rest of November amid the 2026 movie schedule, I wonder if this might be the last week we see the fantasy romance flick and Street Fighter on the Top 10 list.

Honestly, the same could be said about Godzilla Minus Zero as well. I Play Rocky, How To Rob A Bank, Ebenezer and the star-studded Paper Tiger are all just lurking around the corner, waiting for Thanksgiving weekend and people eager to step away from family events to sit in the comfort of their local theater. At the end of the day, I think the consumer is winning, because there will be plenty of great movies to watch in theaters at the end of this month.

For those wanting to see Godzilla Minus Zero but still have yet to see the original, know that Godzilla Minus One is available to stream with a Netflix subscription. I'm in that camp and need to catch up so I can see this acclaimed kaiju movie before it leaves theaters.

#3743. DC Comics movies may undergo yet another reset with James Gunn and Peter Safran replaced by former MCU producer

James Gunn and Peter Safran are out as the co-CEO’s of DC Studios, the main team behind projects like Superman, Clayface, Lanterns, and Peacemaker.

The duo are being replaced by Jeremy Latcham, who made his name at Marvel Studios from the very beginning, working under Kevin Feige. And so, it appears that DC’s new overlords at Skydance after its merger with Paramount are looking for some more money out of this whole situation.

“James and Peter began a new era for DC Studios, guiding it through a major transformation and bringing audiences fresh chapters of beloved stories, including Superman, Lanterns and Creature Commandos,” Skydance CEO David Ellison said. “We’re grateful for the passion and care they brought to this work, and for the lasting mark they’ve left on DC.”

Gunn and Safran’s approach to creating self-contained stories rather than an interconnected MCU-like universe had varying returns, but the duo will end their tenure on Dec. 1 before continuing on in their roles for Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow. Anything beyond that is still a question.

“We’re thrilled to welcome Jeremy to DC Studios,” Ellison continued. “As part of the founding team behind the Marvel Cinematic Universe, he helped define the modern superhero movie and powered some of the biggest, most beloved comic book adaptations of our time. We can’t wait to see the stories he’ll bring to life, and how he’ll help build the future of DC for fans everywhere.”

Latcham’s resume is strong, joining Marvel Studios all the way back in 2004 and working in production on such films as Iron Man, Iron Man 2, The Avengers, Guardians of the Galaxy, Avengers: Age of Ultron, andSpider-Man: Homecoming. He will “will lead DC’s film, television and animation slate, overseeing the creative pipeline, along with production, talent and strategy,” according to The Hollywood Reporter.

“DC’s pantheon of characters is among the most iconic in American popular culture,” said Latcham in a statement. “I’ve had the privilege to help bring some of the most celebrated superhero stories to life on the big screen, and I’m excited and honored for the opportunity to now lead DC Studios into its next era. The chance to steward the incredible cast of DC characters to the screen in a way that excites lifelong fans while introducing their timeless stories to the next generation is a massive responsibility that I do not take lightly.”

And so DC fans are left wondering what’s next, again, after seemingly yet another reset following Gunn taking over from Zack Snyder’s “SnyderVerse” set of films that were extremely hit or miss (mostly miss).

Will Latcham continue on the path that Gunn and Safran began, or will we get yet another do-over? Don’t forget, DC Studios still has The Batman: Part II releasing next year (in theory), and who knows if that’s its own thing or connected or otherwise. Five years between Batman movies should not happen, but, alas.

“Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision, Gunn and Safran said in a joint statement. “In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with Peacemaker, Creature Commandos, Lanterns and Clayface. “We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with.” Gunn had a whole lot more to say on Threads.

I think Gunn and Safran deserved more time to build something special, because Superman was great, Clayface was well-received and turned a profit on a small budget, and fans seem to love Lanterns as well. I always felt like there doesn’t need to be a massive, MCU-like interconnected universe with post-credits scenes in DC, but it appears that Skydance feels differently.

While Hallmark’s Countdown to Christmas lineup is my usual go-to when I’m looking for a holiday rom-com, Hulu released The 12 Dates of Christmas, which has the potential to beat out the best Hallmark and Netflix movies this year.

The 12 Dates of Christmas follows Christina, a workaholic shop owner who has spent most of her life prioritizing her professional life over her personal life. Determined not to show up to her family’s holiday dinner single, Christina lets her best friend organize twelve dates leading up to Christmas to hopefully find her “Mr. Right.” While I don’t want to give away any major spoilers, this is a holiday romance movie, so Christina does eventually find her Mr. Right; it just takes a bit of time.

Directed and co-written by David Lipper, this holiday movie debuted on November 6th and has already climbed the ranks of Hulu’s Top 15 Movies list, sitting in the number two spot. As of this writing, it’s being beaten by Super Troopers 3, which fell short at the box office, but is now finding its audience on the streamer like other recent box office flops.

While The 12 Dates of Christmas didn’t have much competition in the new holiday movie genre on Hulu, it was up against some heavy hitters on the other platforms. Over on Netflix, the book-to-screen adaptation of A Dog’s Perfect Christmas starring the likes of Dennis Quaid and Milo Ventimiglia, dropped on November 4th, and it's currently sitting at number two in the platform's most-watched movies list. Meanwhile, Hallmark released two new original movies, Merry Memories and Holiday Unplugged.

It’s Still October, But I Think I Found My Favorite Hallmark Christmas Movie Of 2026

Unfortunately, there’s no definitive way to tell how well The 12 Dates of Christmas fared against the other new releases. However, given that it’s sitting in the number two spot on Hulu, there’s a reasonable chance it would have beaten or tied for viewership with the other new releases.

After all, one of the major selling points of the holiday flick is that it serves as a mini reunion for Pretty Little Liars stars Lucy Hale and Ian Harding. They famously played the romantic duo Aria Montgomery and Ezra Fitz on that series and at the teen drama show’s peak, the two were a fan-favorite pairing. However, fan opinion has soured over the years, as Ezra was Aria’s high school teacher when they started dating. Still, Harding and Hale always had amazing chemistry, so it’s no surprise they’ve gone on to star as romantic leads once again.

It also helps that Hale has a successful history of playing the lead in mid-budget rom-coms like Prime Video’s Puppy Love or the film adaptation of The Hating Game. Harding is also no stranger to the rom-com world, having starred opposite the Queen of Hallmark, Lacey Chabert, earlier this year in Lost in Paradise. He also starred in what I considered to be Netflix’s best holiday movie of 2024, Our Little Secret, with Lindsey Lohan.

So, if you’re in the mood for a Christmas flick, are tired of all the usual best Christmas movies and have access to a Hulu subscription, definitely give The 12 Dates of Christmas a try. It'll make for a nice watch as you prepare for your own holiday festivities.

Here’s your chance to own a part of automotive & gaming history! We’re incredibly proud to have partnered with Rockstar Games® to bring the custom in-game Grotti Cheetah from ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ to life. See the full details: https://t.co/kakQSnoh96 pic.twitter.com/2CkYUtjEqF

PlayStation 6 is coming and it’s not coming cheaply. Sony is making “solid progress in preparing for the next-generation platform,” the company said last week, but its next-gen device is also reportedly likely to cost over $1,000. ExâPlayStation executive Shawn Layden would prefer the PS6 innovate on price rather than power.

“I think we have enough power in the machine,” the former chairman of SIE Worldwide Studios told The Trophy Room in a recent interview. “The innovation needs to come not from making PS6 for $1,200âit’s to make another PS5 for $300. Now, that would be true innovation.”

Layden has been a critic of the console war arms race in recent years, arguing that improvements have become increasingly hard to spot with the naked eye while sitting in anything less than pristine viewing conditions. The price tags for these improvements have also skyrocketed. Not only has the price of the PS5 actually gone up during its life cycle, the budgets for triple-A studios have exploded even as sales stay flat or go down, leading to a crisis among big publishers.

“I mean, the the jump from PS1 to PS2 was incredible, right?” he said. “And the jump from compact disc to DVD, different storage medium, higher density, and then from two to three when you got to 1080p and you can really do 60 frames per second at uh, you know, at a high frame rate. He used to sell gaming GPUs, now he's in the middle of a geopolitical quagmire.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair in a statement published on Nvidia's newsroom. A strange move for the $4.5 trillion company without the added context: the person he's suspected of having an affair with has also been deemed a Chinese intelligence asset by US officials, and was investigated for smuggling none other than Nvidia's own chips.

The story goes far deeper than Huang's affair; revolving around national security, export controls, spying, chip smuggling, and US/China relations. It's in large part about AI, and who controls the hardware that makes it possible. So, if you're wondering why Huang might be the target of Chinese intelligence to begin with, or why he's announcing his affair in the most public way possible, here's how we got to this point.

Nvidia is at the centre of the debate about whether the United States should sell its most technologically advanced chips to China. The US had already ensured China couldn't make the most cutting-edge chips through a ban of Netherlands-based ASML's chipmaking machines. Yet it has also moved between qualified bans of high-performance chips, leading to made-for-China GPUs, such as the RTX 4090D, RTX 5090 D, and H20; to outright bans, namely the ongoing restrictions for the Blackwell architecture; Nvidia's latest and greatest.

There have been a lot of changes to export controls between the US and China, going back to Biden's trade war. Limitations were introduced in 2023 that used "weighted teraflops" and "adjusted peak performance" to decide which systems were deemed too good to be sold in China. It also limited specific cards based on their total processing power and performance density, which nixed specific chips such as the RTX 4090 (and later the RTX 5090).

Both Nvidia and AMD had to build slower versions of their GPUs to try to keep revenue flooding in from China. This itself was a contentious move, with then-Secretary of Commerce, Gina Raimondo, saying "if you redesign a chip around a particular cut line that enables them [China] to do AI, I'm going to control it the very next day." They went back and forth on this approach a lot.

The good news for Nvidia and AMD was that it was President Trump who eased controls on GPUs, such as the H20 and MI308. Both chips were pared-back versions of existing chips, H200 and MI300, respectively, for the Chinese market in order to meet restrictions. The bad news was Trump said he'd do it in return for 15% of their China revenue. That was in August, 2025.

Whether either company sold any chips to China around that time is another matter, their respective CEOs suggest few, if any. Jensen Huang said in October, 2025, Nvidia was "100% out of China… we went from 95% market share to 0%."

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

AMD's CEO, Dr. Lisa Su, said in the company's Q3 earnings at the start of November that it had received licenses from the Commerce Department but that it hadn't included any sales in its Q4 guidance as it was still up in the air.

By December, 2025—yes, that's how quickly these things change—Trump eased controls on China again, allowing Chinese companies to make do with last-generation GPUs, such as the H200. To get their hands on them requires a thumbs-up from the US Department of Commerce in return for a 25% fee. One report suggested that Chinese firms were limited to 75,000 GPUs each, which was reportedly half of what shopping giant Alibaba and TikTok owner ByteDance had hoped for. Though Nvidia confirmed later that it had received orders from "many customers in China".

This has proven a contentious move. Not only in the US, where national security concerns are paramount, not helped by reports that the US is approving sales to companies with empty offices and ties to possibly blacklisted entities; but also in China. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) wasn't sure it even wanted the GPUs. It took a while to approve imports of the H200 and that wasn't even the end of it, as there was reportedly another hold-up for imports later on.

The CCP didn't sit back and watch this all unfold without action. It jumped between a policy of lessening reliance on US tech, building its own lithographic DUV and EUV machines, and making more efficient AI models, and blocking sales of specific cards, including blocking the RTX 5090 D v2 in China the day Jensen Huang was visiting. That sends a signal. Chinese authorities even launched an antitrust investigation into Nvidia's acquisition of Mellanox, which was linked to export restrictions and part of the tit-for-tat trade war between the two countries at various points in the past half-decade.

Long story short, and to cut out some of the bits where it wasn't really clear which chips could go where and to whom, there was a long period of time when Chinese firms couldn't officially get their hands on a lot of the most powerful GPUs.

Throughout this entire period of export restrictions and policy changes, there were claims that companies and criminals were bypassing the whole lot of it.

Falsifying customs documents, diverting through third-countries, and purchasing under false pretences are all ways that one might get around the ever-changing export restrictions in both the United States and China.

The US Department of Justice seized more than $50 million worth of Nvidia GPUs from an American business attempting to circumvent export restrictions. Alan Hao Hsu, of Hao Global LLC, pleaded guilty to smuggling at least $160 million worth of Nvidia H100 and H200 GPUs between October '24 and May '25. Hsu and others are said to have used falsified shipping paperwork to try to ship the GPUs to China, Hong Kong and elsewhere in violation of US export controls.

More recently, Malaysian customs shared it had seized $12 million worth of chips found in servers, which were headed for undisclosed countries in Asia. This is a hot topic for the US, which previously noted that it wants Malaysia to keep a close eye on shipments of any and all Nvidia chips in and out of the country, for fears of them ending up in China. A similar case saw two Chinese nationals arrested for exporting tens of millions of dollars worth of chips through Malaysia between October 2022 and July 2025.

A known name in datacentres, Supermicro, has also been mixed up in smuggling claims. The company's co-founder, employee, and a contractor were charged with conspiring to divert servers containing powerful AI chips to China, via a Southeast Asian country, in violation of export controls.

“The indictment unsealed today details alleged efforts to evade US export laws through false documents, staged dummy servers to mislead inspectors, and convoluted transshipment schemes, in order to obfuscate the true destination of restricted AI technology—China,” said John A. Eisenberg, Assistant Attorney General for National Security.

The contractor involved in the case pleaded guilty to the charges in a New York court in October, 2026. The Taiwanese authorities were also heavily involved in the case, working with Supermicro to investigate the company's local offices.

There have been similar cases in Singapore, too, which is one of the largest markets for Nvidia outside of the US, despite not making up a similar share of actual shipments. Companies use the country as a base for operations beyond its borders. The Singapore government said at the time it would enforce export controls and combat smuggling.

Whether these chips end up in China is, of course, the big question. The US has questioned whether major AI models out of China, namely DeepSeek, were trained on Blackwell GPUs despite export controls, suggesting it expects some cards are making it through its ban.

Jensen Huang never named the person that his affair took place with, but he does note the national security concerns arising from it, which alongside previous reports, suggest they are Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le. Alice Huang is connected to this saga not only through a personal relationship with Jensen Huang, but how the US authorities came to believe they were a Chinese intelligence asset in the first place.

I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Alice Huang is linked to Singapore-based datacentre company Megaspeed. US authorities were monitoring her on suspicion of chip smuggling—yep, the thorn in the side of the US' export controls—and the company has faced scrutiny over who funds/owns it and its operations; scrutiny that Nvidia has rallied against in the past.

"We want to be absolutely clear: over the past six months, our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia, and Nvidia. These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," a statement on the Megaspeed website reads. It is dated December 23, 2025, and pops up automatically when you visit the page.

Megaspeed rents computing power to other companies and has been connected to Chinese giant Alibaba. There's quite a tangle of connections here, but it's said that Alice Huang used her connections with Alibaba to secure investment, alongside suggestions of securing US chips. Alibaba is also said to have lent money to a Megaspeed subsidiary, Speedmatrix, via its own subsidiary, Apex Enterprise Solutions. Megaspeed's balance sheet grew from $33 million to $3 billion in 2024, reportedly via its subsidiary, the Financial Times reports.

The authorities came to the conclusion that Alice Huang was acting on behalf of the CCP. They also discovered her relationship with Jensen Huang. Though the details of that relationship were not made explicit in the original report by the NYT. Reportedly, Huang had not been briefed on the threat of foreign intelligence, despite his importance and ties to the president of the United States.

Nvidia pushed back on the claims at the time. An Nvidia spokesperson said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year."

The Nvidia Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Nvidia also holds that accusations of chip smuggling made against Singaporean firm Megaspeed were "thoroughly investigated and debunked last year."

We now know that Jensen's relationship was not as usual or as one might expect of a business partnership. A follow-up report from the NYT suggests that a memo was circulated around the Trump administration last spring (slightly unclear when exactly) that suggested a Chinese spy was close to Nvidia's CEO.

All of which leads to Huang's sudden announcement of his affair on Nvidia's newsroom, and the company's simultaneous investigation into the alleged interference by a foreign intelligence asset.

Prior to his statement, Huang had been asked to attend a closed-door joint meeting with the House Select Committee on China, House Foreign Affairs Committee, and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. The meeting would be to discuss the concerns of these committees' in regards to Huang's relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia's security protocols.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” the chairmen say in the meeting invite. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk.”

The meeting is set for November 18, 2026.

So, it's not all about Huang being so open as to express his affair to the world in the most public way possible. It was probably going to come out at some point anyways, and Huang is getting ahead of it to buttress his own chances of survival and his company's share price.

Nvidia's share price has dropped 16% in the past five days; the drop likely coincides with the joint statements from Huang and the Nvidia board, but partially in line with a wider sell-off in tech stocks. The AI bubble is straining right now.

#3737. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang under investigation after admitting affair with alleged Chinese spy in company-wide email

"There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

Nvidia's board of directors has launched an investigation into its own CEO Jensen Huang, after a report by the New York Times claimed he had been participating in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to having an affair in a company-wide statement, apologising to his wife as well as to Nvidia employees. Following this acknowledgement, independent investigators are looking into whether or not he's been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort".

Per the New York Times article, the alleged spy was named as Megaspeed executive and Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang or Huang Le. Jensen Huang wrote in his internal letter: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

With regard to security concerns surrounding the CEO of US-based company Nvidia potentially sharing information with a spy, Huang confirmed that the Nvidia board of directors had initiated an investigation. He added: "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully." The Nvidia board has said it has "no reason to believe either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."

Huang will remain CEO of Nvidia while the investigation is conducted. The New York Times report also claimed that US government officials did not believe Huang knew of Alice Huang's alleged intelligence activities for China.

Following the internal letter from Jensen Huang, Nvidia stock took a tumble from $162bn to $150bn. Nvidia, a juggernaut in the video game hardware industry, is also a key player in the global generative AI industry, which is currently carrying the US economy as other sectors struggle. The company is responsible for AI technology like DLSS 5, which generates lighting, shadows and more using generative AI.

Concerns around the Chinese AI sector passing the American industry has been a core argument against AI development slowdown or regulation, and it's also why Huang's affair may be a matter of national interest.

#3736. A California airplane got evacuated when a passenger playing Call of Duty was overheard talking about a bomb

You can't just say "bomb" on an airplane.

There really is a proper time and place for things, gamers. Please know that when you’re taking your sweaty callouts into public places.

An avid Call of Duty player reportedly caused their plane to be evacuated last night after they were overheard making callouts, according to CBS News. The Frontier Airlines flight was preparing to take off from Ontario International Airport when a complaint was filed.

The complaint, from another passenger on board, said that they heard someone say words “bomb” and “explosion” and then reported it to the crew. The plane then had to be evacuated and the gamer in question was detained.

The CoD-head was ultimately detained and then had to explain to authorities that “bomb” and “explosion” were used to describe his gameplay, as he was playing the game while on FaceTime with a friend and making callouts mid-match.

I’m normally a big proponent of communication in online games, especially shooters like CoD where teamwork is paramount. Maybe just…not while on an airplane, huh? It’s unclear what CoD game the player was enjoying, but it could’ve been the new Modern Warfare 4 now that it’s portable and playable on the go with Nintendo Switch 2.

And when it comes for saying “bomb” on an airplane, it’s probably not the smartest idea. Traveling is stressful enough and people are on edge, so no matter how silly you may think the other passenger was being, I understand it. Plus, all I can really think of is this one scene from the Ben Stiller/Robert De Niro classic comedy, Meet the Parents:

CBS News said crews swept the plane and found no bomb or explosive device on board, thankfully. There was no word about whether or not the CoD player and his friend won the match in question, although I don’t think the rest of the people on that plane really cared.

Owlcat Games has revealed a release date for its tactical role-playing sequel Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy. The game arrives 28th January, 2027 on PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S/X. A Switch 2 release date will be provided "at a later date", a press release says.

Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy follows the good work laid down by Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader a couple of years ago. There's a beta that's been running for a while that offers a complete first Act to try, and it's accessible if you buy a Founders edition of the game. This beta, incidentally, disappears 7th January, when Owlcat prepares the game for launch.

Meanwhile, Owlcat is making a substantially different RPG based around the popular Expanse license - a game that's much more closely inspired by Mass Effect. When I was watching Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, a project on the 2026 movie schedule that features a lot of talk about death, I couldn’t help but think about how often some of its stars have died on screen. Specifically, Steve Buscemi has famously kicked the bucket in a ton of projects, and Sam Rockwell has had his fair share of deaths (and kills) too. So, I asked them about all this, and I was shocked that they had very different takes on the matter.

While Steve Buscemi is on the record saying that the on-screen death that amused him most was his death in The Big Lebowski, I asked him who he was most excited to be killed by. He had a pretty great answer too, as he said:

I mean, Tony Soprano. That was a good one. Coen Brothers have done their best, too.

Listen, to die in such a classic TV show like The Sopranos (which you can watch with an HBO Max subscription), and at the hands of Tony Soprano himself, is pretty epic. Plus, as Buscemi mentioned, the Coen Brothers sure have done their best to creatively kill him too. Honestly, it’d be an honor to die on screen at the hands of any of these guys.

However, despite all this, and the fact that Buscemi has died in movies and TV shows what feels like countless times, he’s actually not a huge fan of watching that kind of thing. He brought that up in our conversation when I asked him to reveal something surprising about himself:

I'm pretty squeamish. I don't like watching violence, including my own death scenes. But you know, it's an occupational hazard for me.

Well, while it’s an occupational hazard for him, his Wild Horse Nine co-star, Sam Rockwell, has a totally different take on what it’s like to die on screen.

**Now, beyond this point there are major, and I mean MAJOR, spoilers for Wild Horse Nine. Please continue reading with caution, and go see the movie in theaters. **

Now, ironically, in the critically acclaimed Wild Horse Nine, Sam Rockwell’s character, Lee, is responsible for multiple deaths, including MJ’s, who Steve Buscemi plays, and Chris’ (John Malkovich). However, while the Oscar winner survived this film, he’s died in plenty of other projects, so I asked him about his favorite way he’s died and his favorite person he’s killed. Here’s what he had to say:

Whoa, favorite person I've killed, and favorite movie I've died? I died in Seven Psychopaths. That was pretty fun. Favorite person I've killed is probably John.

Well, notably, while Buscemi called dying on screen an “occupational hazard,” Rockwell was throwing around “fun” as his primary adjective. However, his death in Martin McDonagh’s Seven Psychopaths is objectively “pretty fun”. I mean, it involves a standoff, Rockwell’s Billy getting shot by Woody Harrelson’s Charlie, and one very memorable moment with a Shih Tzu.

Moving on from that, though, he said his favorite person to kill on screen was John Malkovich, which happens in Wild Horse Nine at the very end of the movie. While it’s by no means a fun scene, it is a very meaningful one, and when I asked Malkovich what it was like to be killed by Rockwell, he said:

Well, there you have it, sometimes dying on screen is fun, sometimes it’s great, and other times it's hard to watch. However, no matter how they react to it, all these guys are remarkable actors who are very good at being both alive and dead in the movies.

So, if you’d like to see them do all that, you can catch Wild Horse Nine in theaters now.

TCL CSOT (the subsidiary of TCL that manufactures OLEDs and other panels) says its new inkjet-printed OLED factory has "entered the equipment move-in phase" (via TechPowerUp) after the project "progressed at a rapid pace". In other words, it's started filling up its production facility with the equipment to produce inkjet OLEDs. Production, the company says, is targeted for about this time next year.

What's the big deal, you ask? It all comes down to that phrase, "inkjet-printed". Inkjet printing (IJP) should be a much more cost-effective way of making OLED panels, which means it should ultimately deliver OLED gaming monitors that are cheaper than traditionally manufactured ones.

Which is saying something, considering how much traditionally manufactured OLEDs have dropped in price over the past year—you can currently pick up a 240 Hz OLED monitor for just $269 at Walmart, for instance. Having OLEDs even cheaper than this will be a whirlwind of fresh air in the current very expensive PC hardware market.

IJP should give us such cheaper panels because the way it makes OLEDs doesn't involve as much wastage. Normally, you have some OLED materials moving through a mask, and some of them are lost. With IJP, however, the materials are printed directly onto the substrate, meaning there shouldn't be any lost materials. Thus, more efficient and cost-effective production.

We'd already heard from third-party sources that this production facility would be producing such cheap OLEDs before long. But that source predicted a start to production in 2028, and TCL is here saying it's targeted for even sooner, in the fourth quarter of 2027.

Whether it ends up being 2027 or 2028, I'm still here for it. We can do with all the good news we can get for PC gaming prices, given the ongoing global memory shortage. Monitors and peripherals seem to be where it's at, and you certainly won't hear me complaining about cheaper, punchy, low-latency displays. Roll on 2027.

#3732. I’ve Played Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Way Too Much To Enjoy The Remake As Much As It Deserves

Game DiaryRemakeSwitch 2The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

I’m not sure exactly how many times I’ve played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but it’s a lot. Back in the days of the Nintendo 64, we weren’t drowning in new releases or free-to-play forever games. You played what you had. And if what you had was good, you played it again and again.

Ocarina of Time was very good and I probably played it a couple of times a year. The remake is gorgeous. It’s also more faithful than I was expecting. I’ve gone through these motions before. Never like this, but enough to not feel as impressed as I should be.

I’m currently making my way through the Gerudo Fortress. My kids and I took turns throughout most of the weekend (I may have had a habit of passing the controller every time we had to go back to the Temple of Time, transform back into Young Link, and run back across Hyrule Field to unlock the next step in a quest). I’ve shown them the original game, but they still feel like this is something completely different. I wish I could feel the same.

I don’t remember every secret in the game and I was never much of a completionist. I would be useless trying to unlock the Biggoron Sword without a guide. But all of the beats along the critical path remain surprisingly familiar, pushed to the forefront of my mind as I encounter each one in the remake. The many ways in which the new version has been streamlined have only served to further that feeling of going back through the motions. The tightly orchestrated logic of the puzzles also reinforces that.

These motions should not be underestimated. The controls are responsive and satisfying. The landscapes are beautiful. And the fundamental gameplay loops remain beyond reproach. Ocarina of Time serves as the foundational blueprint for 3D dungeon puzzles in Zelda. Nearly 30 years later, they still feel remarkably clever, but my fondness for them is closer to the kind of nostalgic recognition I might feel while looking back through the handwritten notes in an old yearbook. You kinda had to be thereÂ back in 1998 to get the full effect.

Being there in 2026 with the remake, I’m surprised just how much of the original has been kept intact. While fans pore over all of the minute differences and pick apart the changes, I’m just a little bit disappointed by how much doesn’t feel new. The combat is mostly the same. The enemies function very similarly. And the side content appears to be more or less the same from the original.

If I didn’t already know the contours of everything you can do in the game, I’m sure it would be thrilling to be discovering all of the arcane secrets and connections for the first time (my kids would rather play friendslop). But with no Master Quest mode at launch, or additional bonus dungeons that iterate on modern design sensibilities and all of the lessons Nintendo has taught players in the intervening 28 years, the overall experience has been a bit hollow for me.

Nintendo may be planning to add that type of thing in future DLC. I’m not sure there’s any benefit to waiting, especially when the magic of sweeping millennial nostalgia is in full force at launch. For now I’m delighted but conflicted. I’d recommend the Ocarina of Time remake as the best way to play the game without reservation. I just wish more of it felt like the first time playing Ocarina of Time. But that’s my problem, not the game’s.

#3730. Hollow Knight Silksong physical editions mention multiple "free content packs" incoming, and call Sea of Sorrow a "giant expansion"

More than a year after its initial release, physical versions of Hollow Knight: Silksong are finally arriving on players' doorsteps. It's the same brilliant and sometimes thrillingly cruel Metroidvania Eurogamer gave five stars to, except this time a pack-in booklet seemingly reveals the existence of multiple "free content packs" alongside the Sea of Sorrow DLC.

Hollow Knight: Silksong's physical editions were originally set to be delivered from 10th November, but some early handovers have given us a peek inside the box. Redditor Me_975 posted pictures of their Nintendo Switch 2 Edition, and there's a few interesting tidbits tucked away - most notably in the manual's chapter on Content Packs.

"The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," the booklet reads. "Prepare for even more adventures filled with new friends, new abilities, and new ferocious foes!"

Developer Team Cherry confirmed plans for post-launch Silksong support last year, but remained pretty tight-lipped about what exactly that would look like. The indie outfit then announced the nautically themed Sea of Sorrow expansion, though we now have proper confirmation there's more content packs still to come, which shouldn't be a huge shocker considering all the free post-launch love Hollow Knight (the first one) received.

Speaking of Sea of Sorrow, that's mentioned here too: "In the first giant expansion, voyage across and beneath a salt-stricken ocean brimming with mystery and menace."

Sea of Sorrow's original release window was a vague 2026 - time's a-ticking, Team Cherry. Still no release date so far, but the booklet does say it's "Coming Soon." Of course, Team Cherry are quite infamous for working on games until they balloon wildly out of control. After all, Silksong was once upon a time intended to be a Hollow Knight DLC, but with games this detailed, I can't really complain about waiting a little extra.

If you are interested in owning Silksong physically, it comes with a big map of Pharloom and the rest of the booklet also includes some really lovely art seemingly ripped straight from the game, as well.

#3729. God of War: Ragnarok is reportedly the highest-earning PlayStation Studios game this generation, but Marvel's Spider-Man 2 isn't far behind

God of War: Ragnarok is the generation's best-selling and highest-earning PlayStation Studios game, according to a new report, but the full top 10 list has a few nice surprises.

In the four years since its PS5 release and two years since its PC port, God of War: Ragnarok has reportedly sold just over 20m copies and generated $1.4b in revenue, according to estimates from Alinea Analytics. About 27.5 percent of the 15m copies it sold on console came from physical editions, and the action blockbuster apparently sold a further 1.1m this year alone. Not bad, boy.

Those stats should bode well for the series' next romp God of War: Laufey - which sees Faye take the spotlight across a multi-mythological afterlife and was recently delayed into May 2027 - even if PlayStation moves away from PC ports for its signature single-player games.

Kratos and Atreus only narrowly beat out perhaps the biggest superhero of them all: Marvel's Spider-Man 2, a game that reportedly made a whopping $1.3b off 19.1m copies across PS5 and PC. The Spidey sequel should keep swinging even higher as the years chug on, though - the report states that sales always surge during the holiday months, and this year's big screen behemoth Spider-Man: Brand New Day led to an even bigger spike than usual.

Racing sim royalty Gran Turismo 7 ($841m), bug-squashing phenomenon Helldivers 2 ($786m), robo-dino sequel Horizon: Forbidden West ($485m), vengeful spirit sim Ghost of Yotei ($410m), undead remake The Last of Us Part 1 ($341m), multidimensional romp Ratchet and Clank: Rift Apart ($334m), Stellar Blade ($316m) and delightful throwback Astro Bot ($292m) round out the top 10 games published by PlayStation Studios this generation.

It's worth noting that Helldivers 2 and Stellar Blade were developed by studios outside the PlayStation umbrella, but the console maker still published both upon release. Ghost of Yotei's performance is also particularly impressive since Sucker Punch's sequel has only been out for a year and didn't get the benefit of a PC port, like many of its PS5 siblings. The success couldn't save Sucker Punch from recent layoffs, however.

On PlayStation's decision to kill disc-based physical releases, analyst Rhys Elliott said that the bottom five games in the list together made $281.7m this year alone: "PlayStation wants those numbers to be bigger in the coming years, which is one of the reasons it's killing the disc (alongside the better margins it and publishers get through digital.)"
