#3728. Complete DREADMOOR Walkthrough: Part 1

DREADMOOR is now out in early access, and it presents an interesting tale for you to explore. Set in a dark, murky world, you have to capture different fish, explore locations, and upgrade your boat.

The campaign of DREADMOOR begins with a tentacle knocking you in the water. The story is broken into multiple quests that you can complete.

The opening will lead you to safe piece of land, and your main objective to get your boat. To do so, you’ll have to power up the generator with the fuel. Once you reach the generator, go to the hut right from there. You’ll find the fuel to power up the generator.

Once the generator has been powered up, you’ll unlock the boat, and then start exploring the world of DREADMOOR. Make sure to pick up the Hook Gun as well along the way.

First, we have to head to the Church Settlement. This place will provide you with your first weapon that allows you to clear blockages. Moreover, you’ll also find the first bed where you can sleep for the night to be over.

Next, we set sail for the Trading Post. Here, we will meet the trader and he will task us with some quest. The trader will also provide us with different blueprints to purchase, but that’s something you can ignore for now.

From there, go upwards to patch the hole in the wall in your shelter. Here, you’ll find the Simple Rod, and you can now fish in the waters. But first, sleep on the bed to survive the night.

Once we get the fishing rod, the next task is to open the door to the Dry Dock. Get the required resources, and then speak with the Engineer to open the doors. This will then allow you to clean and upgrade your ship.

Before you can install the upgrades, you’ll also need to clean the polyps from your ship using the water pipe. Then, you can install the upgrades after crafting them with the required resources. To do so, you’ll have to unlock the blueprints first.

This will complete the first part of the game and get you up to date with all the basics.

The Legend of Zelda: Majora's MaskThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

For the past few days, Zelda fans have been looking for anything in the Ocarina of Time remake that might hint toward a similar reimagining of Majoraâs Mask. One of the more compelling pieces of evidence that one is on the way is actually hiding in the gameâs code, where dataminers have also found evidence of Ocarina of Timeâs Master Quest difficulty mode.

Letâs start with the Master Quest, as itâs more straightforward. The mode originated on the 2003 GameCube port of Ocarina of Time and is a more difficult version of the base game with stronger enemies and rearranged dungeons. The Master Quest was playable from the outset on this version of the game, so if you wanted to play a harder version of the game from the outset, there was nothing stopping you. The 3DS remake Nintendo put out in 2011 also included Master Quest, but you could only play it after completing the main game once. So when the Switch 2 remake seemingly omitted it, fans were naturally disappointed. However, dataminer MrCheeze has uncovered what appear to be files for Master Quest in the code, with dataminer OatmealDome confirming it.

âThe data is incomplete, but I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu’s Belly),â they wrote on Twitter. While Nintendo could distribute the DLC for free, I don’t see why they went to the effort to make it be unlocked by DLC instead of just including it in an updateâ¦â

OatmealDome says that as of the current patch, the Ocarina of Time remake code only checks for one DLC, which is referred to as âMQ,â so itâs unclear if Nintendo has any further DLC plans down the line.

Now for the hint that a Majoraâs Mask remake might be coming. This oneâs a bit more roundabout, but YouTuber Austin John Plays has released a video testing out various amiibo figures on the Ocarina of Time remake, and in doing so may have discovered a hint at a future Skull Kid or Majoraâs Mask amiibo figure that could add the titular mask to the game as a wearable piece of equipment.Â

You can watch the video for a breakdown of what most of the Zelda amiibo figures unlock in the remake (itâs mostly consumable items), but through some altering of NFC tags and scanning them, you can essentially scan the not-yet-released Young Link and Young Zelda figures and unlock the masks theyâll let you wear when they launch next year. The NPCs you meet around Hyrule have unique dialogue for both masks, and the video shows a handful of those interactions. However, there is also code for dialogue for an as-of-yet unknown mask that isnât described with a lot of concrete details, but the dialogue that is in the game right now sure does sound like stuff people might say if they saw Link wearing Majoraâs Mask around Hyrule.

In general, the dialogue hints that this mystery mask makes them uneasy, with someone even calling it “otherworldly.” Austin John theorizes that this is dialogue coded in for a future amiibo figure featuring a character from Majoraâs Mask, possibly Skull Kid, and that this amiibo could be coming out alongside a Switch 2 Majoraâs Mask remake.Â

As far as âevidenceâ of a Majoraâs Mask remake goes, itâs definitely the most convincing thing fans have found thus far. The Ocarina of Time remake includes the Happy Mask Shopkeeper, a character who plays a major role in Majoraâs Mask, and he seems to have been modeled to look like he does in the sequel. Now, thereâs more reason to believe Nintendo has something in the works.

Austin John Plays goes so far as to theorize that the Majoraâs Mask remake might already be mostly done, which would be a pleasant surprise, but for now, all we know for sure is that Link seems to be getting some kind of scary mask in an amiibo update at some point.

My favorite Stephen King adaptation is, without a doubt, Stand by Me. Almost two years ago, we here at CinemaBlend lamented that the Rob Reiner-directed movie was leaving Netflix, but now it’s back, and I definitely plan on watching it again with my Netflix subscription. It’s actually been a lot longer than two years since I last saw Stand by Me, and I’m definitely ready for a rewatch of the movie with a now legendary cast including Wil Wheaton, River Phoenix, Jerry O'Connell, Corey Feldman, Keifer Sutherland, and John Cusack. I have a strong emotional attachment to the movie that outshines any other of King’s book-to-screen adaptations.

I was ten years old when Stand by Me was released in 1986, and I was 11 when I saw it. While the kids in the movie were a touch old, as with any 11-year-old, I thought of myself as slightly older than I actually was. That made me right in the sweet spot for the movie. Sure, I was a child of the '70s/’80s, and the characters in the movies were my parents' generation, but I felt a kinship with them. Plus, because they were my parents' generation, I had a direct connection to the 1950s, having heard all the stories about my mom and dad’s childhoods.

That also meant that I connected with the music in the movie. Director Reiner and music supervisor Celest Ray picked some bangers from the early days of rock n’ roll for the soundtrack, and I loved it. I’m sure I heard the soundtrack before I saw the movie, much like another Boomer nostalgia movie, Good Morning, Vietnam. For kids in the 1980s, the soundtracks to movies like Stand by Me were often our first exposure to them.

The ‘80s were a different time, and seeing Rated-R movies way before we ever should have meant that I had seen a couple of King adaptations before Stand by Me. Movies like Firestarter and Cujo were staples of cable TV, and I’d seen both. I’d also been terrified of both. I didn’t even know Stand by Me was based on a King novella until I saw his name during the opening credits. It blew my mind. I thought he wrote horror stories. Stand by Me definitely wasn’t that, although the dog “Chopper” scared me as much as Cujo did.

Stand by Me is the first adaptation from a King story that showed that other side of the author. The one we all know now from movies and books like this one and The Shawshank Redemption. I had no idea he wrote such heartwarming stories to go along with the ones that kept me up at night, like The Shining and Carrie. Before Stand by Me, all the movies based on his books were like those and Maximum Overdrive, which was another movie I saw around this same time and really scared me, like, a lot.

Stand by Me has no horror at all, and nothing supernatural. Just a deeply personal story about friendship that kids of any era can connect with, just like I did. It's one of the best King movies, despite not being what he's most famous for. I can’t wait to watch it again this weekend.

#3725. "Something's really possible" - Mass Effect cast rally around efforts to save the franchise on the first N7 Day after BioWare's closure

I'm Commander Shepard and this is my favorite video on the internet.

This N7 Day was the first without developer BioWare around, but fans of the Mass Effect series didn't let 7th November go by quietly. The community managed to get several notable Mass Effect actors to lend their voice to the increasingly loud 'SaveMassEffect' movement.

In the weeks since BioWare's shock closure and Mass Effect Universe's cancellation, the community-organised We Are Mass Effect group have put up billboards in Times Square, a mobile billboard outside BioWare Edmonton's former office and much more while directing attention to an online petition.

Today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very important message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect. https://t.co/FOp0qp4wBI

And for the series' annual celebration, the group managed to get a sizable portion of the Mass Effect cast to join in. Commander Shepard actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer, original trilogy composer Sam Hulick, Garrus' Brandon Keener, Jack's Courtnay Taylor, Tali'Zorah's Ash Sroka, Thane's Keythe Farley and many more all showed up in a two-minute video to help potentially salvage the series - sometimes in character.

"When we heard about the formal closing of Boware, I felt weirdly hopeful," Hale said in a separate interview with IGN. "I can't explain it. I just got so weirdly hopeful. My first thought, of course, was for the devs and all the people. And then I just closed my eyes and crossed my fingers and I said, 'I feel something's possible. You know, something's really possible.'"

The other half of Commander Shepard, Mark Meer, noted that "this didn't all just happen in the last 10 days." Near yearly layoffs at EA had slowly trimmed multiple BioWare teams down, sometimes even affecting studio veterans who had been at the company for decades.

"A lot of senior writers within the last year or two were let go. People who had been there from the very beginning. Again, people who had built that company from the ground up, who built the bones of it, who made those games that had captured people so much right back from the 1990s," Meer said.

Owlcat has released a new trailer for its coming Warhammer 40K RPG, Dark Heresy. The inquisition and investigation-focused RPG is now slated for a January 28 launch.

We've loved what we've seen of the game so far: Its focus on investigating heresy and closing cases represents something genuinely novel for Owlcat, which until now has focused on fantasies of rulership (with lite 4x/management gameplay) and quite good (and often very challenging) tactical battles.

One problem: I have a largely uncomplicated relationship with Owlcat games, because I've only ever played them a year-plus out from launch. PCG's other RPG heads, like weekend editor Jody Macgregor and online editor Fraser Brown, remain scarred by their experiences with pre-launch, review period Owlcat games. Jody, for example, lost hours of progress while working on his Rogue Trader review, and once told me that Pathfinder: Wrath of the Righteous' extensive combat system "just didn't work" in the pre-release review period.

Hope springs eternal, though, and I'm a glass half-full type of guy. The corollary to Owlcat games launching rough is that they only get better over time, and the studio has done a phenomenal job supporting its games with both patches and massive story DLCs. Rogue Trader's final add-on, Processional of the Damned, is coming out a month from now on December 8, almost three years to the date after Rogue Trader's initial release.

And after Dark Heresy, there's still the matter of The Expanse: Osiris Reborn. Owlcat is taking its own stab at a Mass Effect-style, sci-fi shooter RPG in the popular setting. How the team is juggling two projects of this magnitude (even at a vastly increased team size) is mind boggling, but I'm just happy to be along for the ride. You can currently wishlist Warhammer 40K: Dark Heresy on Steam.

#3723. GTA 6 pre-orders are tracking "well above expectations" and the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two, says CEO Strauss Zelnick

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick noted that pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto 6 are tracking "far above expectations", and is certain that soon "numbers will speak for themselves" when it comes to the game.

Zelnick also promised GTA Online and GTA 5 will continue to receive updates in order to support the "nearly 235 million" units sold to date across "an unprecedented three console generations". The GTA series as a whole has, to date, sold over 480 million units. Karl Statoff, president at Take-Two, adds the launch of GTA 6 will be a "defining moment for the company and global entertainment industry". Zelnick adds, later in a question and answer session, that he expects GTA 6 to "set a new baseline" for Take-Two. "The future's really bright across the board," he notes.

For the next quarter, Take-Two expects to deliver $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion - with "recurrent consumer spending" to raise by 12 percent, driven by "the groundbreaking release" of Grand Theft Auto 6, and expects to see "significant growth for the Grand Theft Auto series", driven by sales of - specifically - Grand Theft Auto 6's Ultimate Edition, which includes add-on content, and that most people are pre-ordering at its $100 price point. That bonus $20 between the $80 base edition and the Ultimate Edition is counted as "recurrent consumer spending", as is part of that massive bump the company has seen.

It also seems that we will see more GTA games - or content, at least - sooner than expected. "We do think that the nature and velocity of the content we'll see from our iconic franchises, including GTA, will look dramatically different over the next decade." It's a vague comment, but assumedly the work done on the engine and backend of GTA 6 means we'll see more content arriving in shorter order than we're used to for the series. This is per an article published by IGN in line with the earning's call going live.

Elsewhere in the earnings call, Take-Two referred to its current setup with its mobile, sports, 'core new IP' and 'core existing IP' as "the strongest development pipeline in the company's history". In terms of new IP, Zelnick directed investors to consider the launches of incoming projects like Ken Levine's mysterious Judas and Project Ethos (which we don't know too much about yet, other than it's billed as a "roguelike hero shooter"). For core IP, 8 sequels and 7 remakes, remasters, and platform extensions.

Buoyed by these plans, Zelnick outlines that he believes that fiscal year 2027 "will be a historic year for Take-Two" as the company is buoyed by "recent and upcoming releases". No prizes for what that's referring to. If you're curious about what sort of numbers we may be looking at here, all you need to do is cast your mind back to 2014, where you will remember GTA 5 made $1bn in just three days.

Supper Mario Broth, the internet’s number one guy for obscure Mario facts, has shared that he’s in failing health but will continue to bring fans Mario morsels to sup upon until the last flag falls. In a post on social media, Brothâwho has not shared his real name and says he prefers to go by Brothâsaid that despite living a healthy lifestyle, he has heart failure and that his prognosis gives him a 2/3 chance to survive a year.

I am scared I will soon not be able to see Mario again. However, I promise that until that day arrives, I will always be here, posting Mario facts. Thank you all so much for your support through the years.

— Supper Mario Broth (@mariobrothblog.bsky.social) 2026-11-08T20:21:37.669Z

Broth also says that one of the symptoms of his heart failure diagnosis is retinopathy, or the slow degradation of his eyesight. “Since being able to see well is fundamental to my ability to both myself research Mario games and compile the discoveries of others, this may affect my ability to run Supper Mario Broth in the future,” Broth said. “But only blindness or death will result in me no longer posting Mario facts.”

In 2024, Broth posted that his blog was in danger of shutting down due to strained finances in the wake of his mother’s passing. After an impassioned plea for help, the internet rallied around Broth, providing him with enough support that he said he’d be able to continue the Supper Mario Broth project indefinitely.

If you’ve ever wanted weird, obscure, fun, or possibly haunting facts about Mario, Supper Mario Broth was your guy. The Nintendo blogger has been around since at least 2012 posting Mario ephemera gleaned from the plumber’s many games, comics, TV shows, movies, advertising materials, and more. Broth is the one who brought us the Yoshi’s Island glitch that will stop the game for 25 minutes. He told us that in Super Mario Odyssey, Bowser gets scared when Mario has his nipples out. He’s also the guy who fucked us all up with the forbidden (though not canon) knowledge that 1-UP mushrooms grow from dead Marios.

He is possibly the only person in the world who loves and knows Mario as much as Shigeru Miyamoto, and potentially losing him is not only a blow to Mario scholarship but the cool gaming internet as a whole.Â

Broth said that despite his prognosis, he will continue to maintain the blog for as long as he can. “I hope with all my (failing) heart that I can continue doing this for years to come,” he said. “And if I should one day stop posting: thank you very much for reading.”

Halle Berry is known for being something of an open book, as she’s shared aspects of her life and career with her fans over the years. Comments shared by the Oscar-winning actor and Hunt suggest they have a firm relationship. And, apparently, that’s carried right through her ongoing custody battle.

For weeks now, Berry and ex-husband Olivier Martinez have been engaged in a legal skirmish, with the latter having leveled accusations against the X-Men star. Berry (via her lawyer) has since vehemently denied the claims and has appeared in court a few times. By her side has been Van Hunt, who’s been photographed walking with her after the court hearings she’s attended. According to Page Six, Hunt has been a major source of support for Berry amid the legal proceedings. The outlet’s insider says this:

Van has really been Halle’s rock through all of this. He’s been by her side throughout the whole custody battle and restraining order situation.

Hunt and Berry began dating back in 2020 and, before long the singer/songwriter/music producer began making frequent appearances in Berry’s Instagram posts. Although these latest comments are from an insider, they do appear to align with what’s been said and shown of Berry and Hunt’s romance. The source went on to drop further claims about what Hunt’s presence has meant for his partner throughout this time:

It’s obviously been an incredibly difficult and stressful time for her, but he’s been such a calming presence and a huge source of strength. He’s been incredibly supportive through everything, and having someone like him to lean on has made a big difference for her.

Halle Berry Shared How She And Van Hunt Happened: 'I'm Convinced I Manifested My Now Partner'

As previously alluded to Berry and Hunt have appeared together in more than a few of the former’s social media posts over the last several years. For example, years back, Berry posted about their outing at the NY Spring/Summer 2024 fashion show, and she’s also shared sweet tribute posts to Hunt. Berry is even far past the point at which she’s comfortable sharing her and Hunt’s Christmas festivities.

It was in 2025 that Hunt proposed to Berry, though both of them confirmed around that same time that the Bruised actress had yet to formally accept it. Berry explained that after having been married three times, she wasn’t eager to jump into another marriage right away. In her estimation, she and Hunt also didn’t need to “validate” their love in any way. However, earlier this year, Berry clarified that she did accept the proposal but that she and her partner had yet to set a wedding date.

Halle Berry and Van Hunt have emerged as something of a fan-favorite couple on social media, so many take comfort in the notion of the latter comforting his lady amid these legal proceedings. And, as for when or where the pair might actually tie the knot, that remains to be seen.

#3720. As investors ask about GTA 6 and AI, Take-Two CEO once again puts faith in dev creativity, states making hit games "remains the purview of human beings"

"Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future."

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick fielded questions from investors after presenting the financial results of the company. One caller was concerned about AI - specifically about the proliferation of AI-powered compilations and decompilations that have been raising piracy concerns for publishers over the past few weeks.

Zelnick notes that "[the video games] business has been largely immune to piracy" thanks to factors like file size, how console ecosystems work, and aspects related to the online nature of the games industry. That said, Strauss continues, there is a threat posed to the industry because of AI. However, he assures listening investors that Take-Two is appropriately scaling its measures against bad faith actors using artificial intelligence.

"We are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And - at the same time, without in any way being cavalier - every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy, [and] this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Zelnick pivots back to AI again later in the call, where one investor once again asks about AI, seemingly keen to learn whether the CEO feels it can provide GTA 6 developer Rockstar with any kind of "competitive advantage" in the games industry. Given Zelnick's previous comments on the subject, his answer was not a complete surprise.

"It's always been true [that technology benefits us]," explains Zelnick. "We've always created our entertainment inside computers with technology. All advances have benefited us, and I don't expect that that will change - in fact, I hope it'll accelerate. I think at the same time, what we're known for [at Take-Two] is the desire to make the best entertainment on Earth. And, more often than not, we have succeeded - and the creativity that drives that success is human creativity harnessing technology. And I think that's what you'll see in the future, too.

"Undoubtedly some of the most recent technological advances that you've seen have made it easier to create assets. Where all that is consistent with the story of our business. When I started in interactive entertainment (longer ago than I would like to say), it was really difficult to create an asset in a computer. Today, it's a whole lot easier - but you know what's not easier? Making a big hit. Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future. And hit creation remains the purview of human beings."

This isn't the first instance of AI skepticism we've seen from Strauss Zelnick. Back in March, he outright rejected the idea that AI can tackle games on the scale of GTA 6. Elsewhere in the call, the Take-Two CEO reiterated how well GTA 6 is tracking as he reasserted pre-order numbers are well above expectations, and promised that the success of the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two's gaming business.

Just four months later, he and many others have been laid off amid ongoing restructurings following David Ellison’s merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. “My chapter with Skydance and Paramount came to an end today with a layoff. Iâm super grateful for the opportunities I was given the past almost 4.5 years,” Ballard wrote over the weekend. “Itâs a sad day for several of my coworkers who were also affected.”

Many other laid-off staff shared the news on LinkedIn as well. “In this tumultuous climate, it’s hard to find great talent and collaborators to help build your next team and game,” lead engineer David Vera, who wasn’t impacted himself, wrote. “The Skydance crew wasn’t let go because of performance or problematic behaviors. #3718. Harrison Butker Booed Loudly After Missing Back-to-Back Kicks Amid Controversy

The kicking woes for Harrison Butker and the Kansas City Chiefs are showing no signs of slowing down.

Butker, 31, was loudly booed by the crowd at Kansas City’s Arrowhead Stadium after missing consecutive kicks in the Chiefs’ game against the New York Jets on Sunday, November 8.

Right before halftime, Butker clanged a 56-yard field goal off the upright. After a penalty to the Jets, however, Butker was given a second chance from 51 yards out, which he also missed.

CBS announcer Jim Nantz reacted to the barrage of boos, noting, “The crowd’s letting him have it.”

The Chiefs ultimately won the game, 35-12, putting an end to their two-game losing streak. Butker missed his only field goal attempt of the game, but was five-for-five on extra points.

In the locker room, Butker acknowledged the negative reaction from Chiefs Kingdom.

“I mean, I’m booing myself sometimes,” Butker said. “The fans are passionate. They want [us] to win games. They want me to make kicks. I want to make kicks. I’ve got to be better.”

He added, “I feel confident, I’m excited for the kicks, and I’ve just got to do better. Week after week, saying the same thing. Guys support me. They’ve seen what I’ve done in my 10 seasons, and they want me to be at my best. I know who I can be. I’ve just got to make them go in.”

Butker insisted he’s not dealing with any lingering issues that are causing his dip in accuracy.

“I feel great,” he said. “I definitely have the distance, the power. It’s just making kicks.”

Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes said the team still has “confidence” in Butker, despite his subpar stretch of play.

“That’s pretty much it,” Mahomes, 31, said after the game on Sunday. “I’ve seen him make field goals at the biggest stages that you can make in this league. I want him to know I have as much confidence in him as I’ve ever had, just trying to give him that vote of confidence.”

In response to Butker’s struggles, the Chiefs signed kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad last month. Tucker, 36, previously served a 10-game suspension for violating the NFL’s personal conduct policy following allegations of sexual misconduct by 16 massage therapists.

Head coach Andy Reid was non-committal about the team’s path forward at the kicking position following the Jets win.

“I’ll address that as we go throughout the week,” Reid, 68, told reporters. “I’ll look at everything. I’m not making any decisions right now.”

The Chiefs travel to Atlanta to play the Falcons on Sunday, November 15.

I fear opening the Pandora's box that is my SSD's health report. I'd much rather live in ignorance until the day it inevitably fails on me. Some eagle-eyed AMD GPU users, however, have spotted their own SSD health dropping much faster than they expected, and have placed the blame squarely on an AMD Adrenalin driver utility.

Redditor Darklinkpower has flagged the issue on the r/pcmasterrace subbreddit. "I just found out that the driver eats up 1% of my SSD health every month for 16 month," says the redditor, "where[as another] user reported losing approximately 1% of their SSD health every month."

The reports come from multiple sources, including the Radeon subreddit, and Tomasz Gawroński on X, who says that Adrenalin driver utility atieclxx.exe had performed 19.5 GB of I/O writes on their machine in just 12 hours. According to Gawroński, the bug has been present since Adrenalin Edition 26.7.1 released in June of this year.

The issue doesn't appear to be present on all machines, and our own AMD GPU-using Jacob Fox hasn't been able to reproduce it. Still, the reports are numerous enough to suggest something is amiss.

In terms of an official response, representative AMD_Matt on the AMD community forums replied to a user flagging the issue last month, saying "We're looking into it with the aim to resolve it in a future driver release." Another AMD representative on Reddit, AMD_Vik, confirmed the disk write issue "should be fixed" in Adrenalin 26.11.1, although no exact release date has been given beyond its expected arrival later this month.

It seems that AMD is well aware of its misfiring utility, so hopefully the fix is on its way. After all, SSDs are bloomin' expensive at the moment, so I, along with the rest of the PC gaming community, are likely going to be eeking out the ones we've got for some time to come.

#3716. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake’s Castle Town Has A Scene That Will Haunt Me Forever

Nintendo Switch 2The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

I’ve been seeing some chatter online about a specific scene in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time that’s extremely beloved by longtime fans. It’s easy to miss: if you visit the Hyrule Castle Town back alleys after Zelda and Impa flee from Ganondorf, but before the time skip, you can find a soldier on the ground slumped against the wall. In the original, if you speak to him, he asks if you’re the “boy from the forest” and, in a pained stutter, tells you that Ganondorf has betrayed the king and that Zelda has escaped, but that she wanted to give something to you before she left.

His final words direct you to the Temple of Time, the text speed slowing as he finishes his line, before he shudders and fully collapses. Trying to speak to him further prompts Navi to say, “He’s not moving anymore….”, and that’s it. The soldier’s dead.

This moment has been cited by many as a prime example (among very many!) of the “darkness” of the original Ocarina of Time. It’s an otherwise noble and normal NPC dying a painful death in a back alley due to the cruelty of the villain, in front of the child protagonist who, up to this point, has only seriously fought soulless monsters. He’s not yet had to face down death in this particularly tragic way.

In the remake, however, the soldier doesn’t die. He stays alive, and you can talk to him as many times as you like to have him direct you to the Temple of Time. I believe this is just one of a cavalcade of examples of Nintendo being terrified that the player is going to get lost in the remake somehow and not know where to go. What if you forget you’re supposed to go to the Temple? He’s there to remind you, again and again, seemingly merely exhausted instead of in agony.

About the soldier in the back alley byu/dampflokfreund inOcarinaOfTime

People are bringing this up as evidence that the remake has somehow blunted the “darkness” of the original Ocarina of Time. Defanged it a bit, suggesting a more modern fear from Nintendo of exposing children to grim themes. I saw people say Nintendo “censored” itself here, or that this may have been related to “ratings.” Setting aside questions over whether or not some vague content meter of “darkness” or “maturity” is the measure of anything really, I want to push back on the idea that this moment in Castle Town has been stripped of its power: the soldier lives, yes. But for me, the remake transforms visiting Castle Town between Zelda’s departure and Link’s first experience of time travel in a way that makes it one of the most haunting and sad moments in the entire game…especially if you know what’s coming.

When you emerge in Castle Town as Adult Link in either game, it’s in ruins. Dark clouds hover over the square, and Hyrule Castle looms ominously, now the seat of Ganondorf’s power. The once-bustling square is now home to multiple horrifying Redead enemies, heavily implying that some the townsfolk may have been transformed into these health-sucking zombies. You can find most of the major NPCs from Castle Town now living in Kakariko Village, but not all of them make it there. The implication is that Ganondorf essentially enacted a massacre on the town before installing himself as king, and only a handful of refugees escaped to tell the tale.

The original Ocarina of Time had some conversationalists in Castle Town right before the timeskip, but many of the NPCs had only a little or even no dialogue, and just served as background to suggest a bustling town square. A few of those characters express some anxiety about the guy on the horse who just galloped through, if you talk to them in the brief window between Zelda’s escape and Link’s transformation. It’s the only time you can hear this special dialogue, but most of it is pretty humdrumâjust folks remarking on the horses that galloped through.

The remake’s Castle Town is populated with essentially all of the same NPCs that existed in the original, but with one key difference: just about all of them will speak to you, and most will do so at length, talking about whatever it is that’s on their mind. In that same short window of town panic right after Zelda has fled, almost everyone’s dialogue changes to remark on what just happened…but with a far deeper awareness of what’s coming than was expressed in the original game. A little girl talks about being told to stay away from the “old man chasing people.” The owner of the dog Richard spends all day and night frantically searching for him. Another wealthy woman demands answers from the guards. Some people, happy that fewer people are outside, go on a shopping spree, while one guy ponders stocking up on supplies in case of disaster. Honey and Darling continue to dance blissfully, deliberately ignoring the sound of horses.

Multiple NPCs discuss leaving town, aware that an occupation of some sort is imminent. One woman in particular suggests she might move to Goron City, but gives up the idea when she remembers she can’t eat rocks, while another puts her foot down: “Cowardsâall of you! I’m not leaving this town no matter what! I love this place.” When asked what she’ll do if the town is overrun by monsters, she stammers that she’ll “figure it out.” Maybe she’ll make friends with the monsters.

Is it weird to say I had to set the controller down for a moment after hearing all this? This whole scene was…a lot. So much more so than it was in the original. I am all-too-aware of many places in real life where people, for years and years, live extremely normal, cheerful lives. Then, something happens. Something off-putting, scary, ominous. Some folks insist everything will be fine. Others panic. Still others double down. And then, the worst thing imaginable, or even something unimaginable. People are made into victims or refugees by some force they had no power or time to stop. Harmony in one moment, horror in the next, and in between the two this tiny, surreal space of half-awareness of what might come, and disbelief that it ever could.

It’s easy to abstract the horror of all this in a video game when it’s zombies and cartoon villains. The soldier dying in the alley was sad and, sure, “dark,” but apart from a curiosity it never did much for me. Now, though, we have this haunting interlude between childhood and adulthood where these characters, briefly, exist in terrified uncertainty. These few minutes of wandering town and speaking with everyone hit me unexpectedly hard in a game that’s otherwise, relative to many other things I’ve played, pretty tame and even childish.

I think the small touch of adding all this dialogue to these NPCs in Castle Town in this moment, a moment most people will totally skip over, was a powerful and good artistic choice made by this new, younger development team. I don’t know about “dark,” I guess, or whether the remake is more so than the original. This scene has convinced me that such designations matter less than they ever did.

#3715. Former NYPD Officer Charged in Fatal Stabbing of Jogger Katie Suarez

A former New York Police Department officer was arrested in connection with the death of Katie Suarez, who was fatally stabbed in the neck while jogging in her Brooklyn neighborhood.

The New York City Police Department confirmed to Us that Sayed Mohassib was arrested on Saturday, November 7, and was charged with murder, tampering with physical evidence and criminal possession of a weapon.

Authorities identified Mohassib, 27, as a suspect after investigators reviewed surveillance footage of the area around the time of the attack, according to NBC News.

The footage allegedly showed Mohassib throwing out trash bags near his residence on the night that Suarez, 28, was killed.

Mohassib allegedly told authorities that he did not remember attacking Suarez though recalled realizing he was covered in blood after the attack, according to NBC News.

It’s not currently clear if Mohassib has entered a plea or retained legal counsel following his arrest. The New York Police Department had no additional updates to share when contacted by Us about the case.

Mohassib was employed as a school aide at an elementary school in Brooklyn at the time of his arrest. A student at the school Mohassib worked at told the New York Post that he was acting “off” in the week leading up to the murder.

“He was acting a little bit, like, I don’t know, weird. A bit off,” the student claimed.

Two other students also spoke to the outlet and claimed that they saw Mohassib talking to himself, while one of the students said that he seemed “nervous” and “worried.”

Following Mohassib’s arrest, the New York City Department of Education confirmed to People that the suspect was an employee of the district.

“The safety of our students is our very top priority,” the representative said in a statement. “We have suspended this individual and will move to terminate employment pending the outcome of the conviction. We are supporting the NYPD in their investigation however is needed.”

The representative added that the department is “providing support and resources to the school community.”

Prior to his role with the school district, Mohassib worked as an employee of the NYPD in 2022. He only served in the role for about a month before requesting to be transferred to the military, a police source told NBC News. The source added that Mohassib was ultimately discharged from military service due to mental health concerns.

Mohassib reportedly requested to rejoin the NYPD in January 2023, but was denied just weeks later.

As Us previously reported, Suarez was jogging on October 30 near a Brooklyn waterfront path on Shore Parkway when she was stabbed two times in the neck around 8:15 p.m. in a seemingly random attack.

Her parents set out to find her when they were unable to get in contact with her, and Suarez was taken to NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn for treatment once she was found injured. Suarez succumbed to her injuries three days after the attack.

This weekend, Saturday Night Live welcomed comedian Druski as its latest host for Season 52, and some serious history was made. On the one hand, there was the fact that Druski became the first social media-birthed star to host SNL. And, on the other hand, I’m not sure I’ve ever seen the long-running sketch comedy series have such an eclectic assortment of stars. Chris Rock was just one of the notable names to show up to root on the Internet celebrity, and I’m shook by this roster of talent.

During Druski’s opening monologue, he was joined by Emma Stone, his co-star in the upcoming comedy film The Catch. The Oscar winner’s appearance was surprising enough on its own and, before that, the new senator-elect of Texas, James Talarico, appeared in the opening monologue alongside James Austin Johnson’s President Trump. The notion of Rock, Stone and Talarico being on the same episode of SNL is wild, but check out the clip from X down below to see all the other big names who appeared during the goodbyes:

Wow, I don't know what the hell is even happening, Dave Chappelle and Chris Rock showed up, with Walton Goggins, Michael B. Jordan and even Austin Butler (left side, blue cap) were there hanging out with Druski! https://t.co/8pRxYQTdTuNovember 8, 2026

I honestly can’t remember the last time I’ve seen such a mix of stars during a single episode of Saturday Night Live, and that’s saying a lot, given the show’s history. Over the years, SNL has treated viewers to some truly jaw-dropping celebrity cameos. It may be fair to say that, in some ways, this latest situation is a bit different, though, given that the bulk of these stars didn’t actually perform or speak. Still, I’m going to have the mental image of that group on stage for quite some time.

Michael Che Pitched The Rock A Black Adam Sketch On SNL That’s Straight Up Filthy

This is actually the second week in a row that SNL has welcomed some guest stars back to its hallowed halls. For the Halloween episode, which was hosted by Inde Navarrette, Tom Hanks reprised his role as David S. Pumpkins. Not only that, but Hanks was joined by series veteran Bobby Moynihan, who returned as one of Pumpkins’ skeletal dancers and as Drunk Uncle. Since then, Moynihan has spoken about hanging out with Hanks ahead of the taping, and I wish I could’ve been a fly on the wall.

In terms of this week’s episode, though, Druski (whose real name is Drew Desbordes) really seemed to make a splash, thanks to sketches like Bubu Mobile and Washington in Focus. The center piece of the episode, though, was arguably Desbordes’ portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes in a wild sketch that parodied the documentary You Can See Everything.

I’m not sure how the show could possibly top an episode like this in terms of star power. Comedian – and former SNL writer – John Mulaney is hosting next week, though, so maybe he and the writers have some surprises up their sleeves. Look out for that when Saturday Night Live returns with Mulaney and musical guest Phoebe Bridgers on November 14 at 11:30 p.m. ET on NBC amid the 2026 TV schedule.

Killing Floor studio Tripwire Interactive has laid off 36 employees in what it says "was certainly not an easy decision, but unfortunately a necessary one for the organization."

The cuts at Tripwire are quite substantial: A source at the studio told PC Gamer that roughly 40-50 employees are left following the layoffs.

"Our team is focused on our internal projects, including active development of Maneater 2, ongoing work on Killing Floor 3, and publishing efforts under the Tripwire Presents label," the studio wrote in a message shared on LinkedIn. "We are continuing to give the best support possible to all of our games and remain committed to our awesome community."

Maneater 2 was announced in September, five years after the release of the original, which was a significant success for Tripwire. But the studio has had difficulty replicating that success, even with its best-known game series: Killing Floor 3, released in 2025, remains mired in "mixed" user reviews on Steam, and its concurrent player count on the platform is a small fraction of its 2016 predecessor.

The layoffs also come less than a week after Tripwire announced an expansion of its Tripwire Presents publishing division to include "scaled publishing support of smaller independent developers"—essentially offering a variable suite of services to what Tripwire publishing director Bryan West called "scrappy developers" who could a little assist with their games in specific areas.

Update, 11/9/26, 1:15 p.m. Eastern:Â Gunn has released a statement on his Instagram account, confirming he is still working with DC on bothÂ Man of Tomorrow and another project he’s writing on. Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios.

When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn’t know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn’t pass up the unique opportunity. I’m glad I took the job.

There have been so many highs along the way – releasing Superman and Clayface, making Peacemaker, reading the scripts to The People Vs, the entire process of Man of Tomorrow, which thus far has been the best filmmaking experience of my life, and numerous other moments.

The highest of the highs have been all the talented and wonderful people I’ve worked with and grown to love: the DC Studios crew, our talented collaborators, our casts and crews, and the boisterous and hilarious fans. And the best part of all has been working with Peter Safran, the smartest and most competent person I know. You’ve been the best partner a person could ask for, and, more so, a truly good friend.

But what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years (Jenn, I love you and I’m sorry and you don’t need to feel guilty for being the happiest of all people that I’m no longer doing this job). And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head.

So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking. That’s not to say Peter and 1 are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we’ve just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing, and we’ll see where it goes after that. And, of course, the characters we set up will live on.

Thank you so very, very much for embracing the characters and stories we’ve put on screen.

#3711. Dad Left 6-Year-Old Asleep in Target Line to Hold Spot for Pokemon Cards: Cops

A South Carolina father left his 6-year-old daughter asleep with a pillow and a blanket in a line outside Target after 1:00 a.m. so the girl could hold his place to buy new Pokémon cards, police said.

John-Michael Dooley later acknowledged to detectives that he went home without his daughter, leaving her in line to “avoid missing the opportunity to purchase the cards,” the Charleston Police Department said in a Friday, November 6, news release.

Dooley, 35, of Johns Island, was arrested on charge of unlawful conduct toward a child after he returned to the Target in Charleston that morning, according to authorities.

Dooley was one of several customers who arrived at the Target in Charleston’s West Ashley district overnight to wait for the release of a new Pokémon trading card set, police said.

He had been waiting in line with his daughter until he left her alone after 1 a.m., witnesses told police.

The child was sleeping alone in line for around an hour, leading to “concerned customers” calling police, authorities said.

Customers identified Dooley as the girl’s father when he eventually returned to the store from his house, according to police.

“The child was unharmed and placed into emergency protective custody with the South Carolina Department of Social Services (DSS),” police said.

It’s unclear whether the girl is still in DSS custody. The agency didn’t immediately respond to an inquiry from Us on Monday, November 9.

Dooley was booked in the Al Cannon Detention Center, where he was held on a $40,000 bond, records show.

He later posted bond on Friday and was released, according to jail records.

Information on Dooley’s legal representation wasn’t listed in court records.

When reached by NBC News, Dooley declined to discuss the circumstances of his arrest in-depth, as advised by his attorney. He told the outlet that news reports had inaccuracies in relation to his arrest on Friday, when the Pokémon Trading Card Game: Mega Evolution — Delta Reign expansion set was released.

Dooley is due in court for his initial appearance scheduled for December 18, records show.

His arrest comes after a Florida mother was taken into custody on a plane for allegedly leaving her four children home alone as she flew to Las Vegas for a work trip in late October, Us previously reported. The children were ages 14, 12, 11 and 9.

#3710. Meet Colleen Allen, the Future of American Fashion

This is the November 4, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

The United States has been overtaken by a blue wave following last night’s midterm elections. James Talarico flipped Texas to make it to the Senate, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire became the first out gay man to be elected to the Senate, and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia is now the first Black woman to be elected governor in the history of the US. There were great memes about what this could mean for the country—largely, the comeback of woke—and some fashion moments worth discussing. Scroll down for a midterm-fashion verdict, including notes on the curious case of a seemingly AI-generated picture featuring Chanel and Valentino products supposedly spotted at a Michigan Democratic Party election night event in support of Abdul El-Sayed.

In other news, Ye is staging a comeback Yeezy show in Los Angeles tonight at the brand’s flagship—keep an eye out tomorrow for a report from my Angeleno colleague Maxwell Adler. Congratulations are in order for Schiaparelli’s Daniel Roseberry, who is having a great week after running the New York City Marathon on Sunday, posting a much-discussed thirst trap on Monday morning, and receiving the Leader in the Arts Award at the Smithsonian’s annual Hirshhorn New York Gala on Monday night. Congratulations as well to the winners and honorees at the 2026 CFDA Awards. More on that very curious evening below, including an interview with Colleen Allen, certified fashion darling and Emerging Designer of the Year winner.

Mentioned in this issue: Jon Ossoff and his tight suit, Colleen Allen, Ralph Lauren, Jill Biden, Melania Trump, Hasan Piker, Zohran Mamdani and Rama Duwaji, and Tim Burton and his new Loewe collaboration.

The CFDA Fashion Awards on Monday night brought some star power to the American Museum of Natural History: Keke Palmer hosted, and presenters included Matt Damon, Cole Escola, Lupita Nyong’o, Laufey, and Demi Moore. And yet the mood of the evening was somewhat tentative. The Council of Fashion Designers of America is under something of a renovation: Steven Kolb, its former CEO, resigned in September following an altercation with PETA protesters at New York Fashion Week. Serving in his stead is Hildy Kuryk, a comms expert who spent four years at Vogue as its executive director of communications following a career in politics. Kuryk is serving as interim CEO and heading up the search for Kolb’s permanent replacement. On Monday night, she stayed out of the spotlight, leaving most of the audience wondering—and gossiping about—who the new face of the CFDA could and should be.

Rachel Scott of Diotima took the main award of the night as womenswear designer of the year, and Anthony Vaccarello, who just left Saint Laurent, was presented with the International Designer of the Year Award by muses Zoë Kravitz, Hailey Bieber, and Rosé. Ralph Lauren was named menswear designer of the year, securing his place as the most awarded designer in CFDA history. Mr. Lauren himself made an appearance—a crowd-pleaser that also left me wondering if the American industry often puts too much emphasis on its past and not enough on its future. In that spirit, I called up Colleen Allen, who took the prize for emerging designer of the year, and asked her to introduce herself to those of you who haven’t met her yet.

Colleen Allen received her award from designer Gabriela Hearst and actor and writer Cole Escola.

José Criales-Unzueta: What would you say is the most important thing for people to know about your background?

Colleen Allen: I often lead with that I always was a menswear designer and was never intending on doing womenswear. That point of view has really guided my work and who I’ve become. I just love the process of making. I did menswear because there wasn’t an identity of women that I saw that I connected with, really, with brands when I was first going to school. And I just loved the craft of tailoring and learning the physical process of cutting a pattern. I think there’s such an ephemerality in making womenswear, in a way. Draping on a mannequin is quite abstract to me. A huge part of my identity is thinking like a tailor.

Where did you go to school, and where did you work before starting your brand?

I did half at Parsons, half at Central Saint Martins. I consider Parsons to be quite technical, and Saint Martins sort of opened up the world conceptually for me and gave me a lot of freedom and thinking about world-building. I was at The Row doing menswear for three years, and then I also interned at Vogue for a minute [and] Calvin Klein 205W39NYC was a very formative experience. When I was an intern there, I was full-time. I was there for eight months, but it was just so cool because it was all in the same room with Raf [Simons, now at Prada], Pieter [Mulier, now at Versace], Matthieu Blazy [now at Chanel]. You knew at that moment how special it was and how crazy it was. I think the world didn’t process it, but when you were in the room, you knew these people were all so important. And so I think being around that every day and absorbing the way that they worked together and they’re such world-builders, all three of them are very conceptual. I think that was a huge informative experience for me.

I think that people know me for color. The feedback that I get from people who buy the clothes is that when you’re wearing a big velvet coat in a color, or even just a dress or a top, people get stopped on the street just because it’s so visually impactful. Velvet is also a signature. That duality of color and texture, and also a bit of a historical Victorian sensibility.

Where do you think that interest in Victorian garments comes from?

There’s an emotional, aesthetic love for it. There’s a bit of a groundedness and a weight to it, and a bit of that period of time was quite spiritual thinking about the afterlife and death, but there was a sense of romance around that that I think really seeped into the clothes in a way that I don’t know if other periods of time really reflect. On the other side of it, it isn’t Victorian specifically, but a lot of historical dress for women is incredible tailoring—thinking about those bodice jackets that have a lot of tiny little panels with lots of little grosgrain finishing on the seams on the inside—and it’s all about molding to the female body. As a menswear designer, I love wearing men’s clothes and wearing a tailored jacket, but I think that the idea of having that sensibility and also reflecting femininity is the perfect storm for me. A lot of that just got lost in a certain period of time once women were able to wear pants, and in the transition of women being able to access menswear, women’s tailoring never got back to that sort of technical level of fitting the body or the female form.

You’ve never done a runway show, which is something that many young designers feel signals their arrival. Why is that?

I love fashion and wanted to work in fashion because I loved watching fashion shows. And specifically, I loved shows that were immersive. I always go back to [Alexander] McQueen [that signaled] fashion is more than product. It is this world-building, cinematic performance art, and you can take it just so much further emotionally. If I’m going to do a show, I want it to carry that level of weight. For me, at my scale, it just feels like the most manageable way to encapsulate a sense of emotion is to do it through a [photo] shoot and showroom appointments for now, just in truly a practical sense. But it is my dream, and I’m working towards having a show. But when I do it, I want it to feel special.

It’s a bit surreal, in a way. It’s especially cool that it’s voted by the industry, and it sounds maybe kind of cheesy, but I do just feel like that is the best reward. That all these people that I’ve worked with are acknowledging [me]. It feels solidifying, grounding. It feels like I’ve been doing this forever, and it’s also going by so fast at the same exact time. It lets me be present and acknowledge myself for how much work has been put into it and that I did it and it’s real and it’s something I dreamed about for so long.

Do you feel like a fashion-industry darling?

[Laugh] Oh my God, how does one answer that question? Gosh, I think that three years ago I was entering these rooms knowing absolutely no one... I think the showroom has actually really fostered real relationships and friendships in the industry, and a sense of community that just feels really good. I work as hard as I can to support whatever the stylists are doing or the editors, I’m always physically running around to make sure that they get the clothes because I love what they do. I love that I know the photographer and the stylist and all the people, and know that if my clothes are in it, it will be amazing for me and they made the effort to reach out to me, to include me in it. The word darling is such an ick word [laugh]. I feel like the word I want to say is camaraderie, because everyone just works so hard. Nobody is flouncing around being a darling. We are all hustling together, and if I can support your hustle and you support mine, that’s the best thing. And when it works, it’s just so satisfying.

Tim Burton, iconoclast filmmaker extraordinaire, has a new capsule with Loewe, which has recreated characters and vignettes from The Nightmare Before Christmas as bags and charms. These kinds of collabs were a staple when Jonathan Anderson was at the brand, and Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez seem to be game to keep them coming with the same endearing whimsy.

In the age of artificial intelligence, the film has become a symbol of human craft and ingenuity. “The more it keeps going that way,” Burton told me yesterday, calling from London and answering a question about the proliferation of AI in film, “the more I appreciate [the human] side of it. I think it’s something that’s very important to keep in the world, the tactile, not being on a screen all the time and doing all that sort of thing. To me, [humanity] is very important to life and art and anything, really.” We also spoke about his collaboration with A$AP Rocky and whether he’d ever do a live-action remake of 2005’s Corpse Bride.

#3709. Zach Cregger Revealed One Part Of His Resident Evil Experience That ‘Frustrated’ Him, And I Get It

Video game adaptations have a way of making everybody angry. However, I can understand why Zach Cregger expected a different conversation around his Resident Evil movie. The director behind Barbarian and Weapons has opened up about the one part of releasing his 2026 movie calendar horror hit that genuinely "frustrated" him, and I get where he's coming from.

During an appearance on The Town with Matthew Belloni, Cregger was asked whether he'd consider tackling another established franchise after Resident Evil. His answer led to a candid discussion about the reaction to his film, which follows Austin Abrams' medical courier Bryan through a nightmare in Raccoon City. Cregger felt people cared more about what he changed from Capcom's games than about the movie itself. He explained:

I think I was frustrated at the conversation around Resident Evil and how much of the conversation really didn't have anything to do with the movie. It had everything to do with whether the movie was living up to the different standards that different fans of the games had, whether it was using the characters or not, or what did I get wrong in the lore, or why is it? It was just a lot about why isn't this like the source material or why is it good that it's not like the [source material].

I can understand why that would be exhausting. After spending years making a new horror movie, you release it into the world, and suddenly everyone argues about why Leon Kennedy isn't included. However, I also empathize with fans who have waited a long time to see their favorite characters properly adapted.

Cregger chose to tell an original story within the Resident Evil universe instead of recreating one of the games, and the movie's biggest strength has nothing to do with lore or Easter eggs. His movie swaps familiar protagonists for Bryan and leans into the sensation of playing survival horror: limited resources, increasingly awful encounters and the knowledge that the next room might be your last. Before release, some fans objected to the missing characters and changes to Raccoon City.

What's interesting is that the movie did incredibly well. Resident Evil has earned more than $400 million worldwide, according to Box Office Mojo, while Rotten Tomatoes lists a 96% critics' score. Early reviews praised RE for its relentless pacing and the way Cregger captured the experience of playing the games.

Still, success didn't erase Cregger's disappointment with the discussion surrounding it. He continued:

All the conversation just felt like it was about not the movie. And I'm proud of the movie. I really love the movie. I should have known better going into it. I should have understood that that was going to be the case, but for some reason I was a little shocked.

That last admission is what stuck with me. Cregger is a fan himself, and he previously acknowledged that players hoping for Leon's story had a fair reason to feel disappointed. But he also wanted people to judge the actual movie he made. Surely there's room for both opinions.

Zach Cregger's not necessarily finished with Raccoon City, either. He told Belloni he'd like some creative input if the series continues, even if somebody else directs the next installment. Personally, I hope he gets that chance. Given how well this one turned out, I'd much rather see what else he dreams up than spend another round arguing about which character didn't show up.

Resident Evil arrived on digital video-on-demand (VOD) platforms to rent or buy on November 3, 2026, so check your favorite streamer for details.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3708. Colorado Woman Sentenced to Prison After Hitting Man, 79, While Driving High

A Colorado woman will spend the next several years in prison after she was convicted for hitting an elderly man with her car while high.

Amy Dalton was sentenced on Tuesday, November 3, to four years in prison after she was found guilty of vehicular homicide while under the influence of a substance.

After she learned her sentence, Dalton, 38, addressed the court regarding her crime. “I will carry the weight of this tragedy with me for the rest of my life. I accept full responsibility … I do not expect forgiveness, but I can ask,” she said, according to The Gazette.

She also shared a message with her son before she was taken into custody. “I love you. I promise that I will be back, OK?” she reportedly said.

Dalton admitted she smoked marijuana and took other drugs before she hit Robert “Bob” Selle with her 2016 Subaru Outback while he was mowing his front lawn on August 24, 2025.

Police said that the victim’s wife, Donna Selle, ran outside of her home and was “talking with” Robert, 79, just moments before he died.

“She was watching him through the front window of their house when she observed a silver car, that appeared to be going too fast, become airborne, [and] hit her husband, sending him flying off the lawn mower,” police reported in the arrest affidavit viewed by Us.

A neighbor’s security camera captured the crash, which showed Dalton’s vehicle flying off the road and hitting Robert as he mowed his lawn.

“Dalton’s Subaru became airborne over the driveway,” the affidavit said. “As the Subaru landed, it collided with a barbed wire fence and then traveled into the yard/field … where it (Subaru) collided with Robert Selle, who was operating a riding lawn mower.”

After Robert was struck, “the Subaru continued overturning in the field, coming to rest on its roof.” Authorities said that Robert “was knocked from the lawn mower and came to rest on the ground near the Subaru.”

Robert was initially responsive “and talking with his wife” after the crash, but he later became unconscious and died at the scene.

“For no obvious reason at the time, Dalton failed to maintain control of the Subaru and the vehicle drifted off the right/west side of the roadway,” the affidavit stated. “After analyzing the Subaru’s ACM [airbag control module] data, it’s clear that Dalton never applied the brakes or applied any evasive steering input in the seconds leading up to the crash.”

Dalton spoke to officers after the crash, who noted there was “a strong odor of marijuana coming from her.” She then admitted that she “consumes marijuana daily” and takes “multiple medications,” as well as shared that she “had recently tried methamphetamine for the first time.”

Authorities said that Dalton appeared “mellow” and was “not very responsive” to EMS questions or treatment, and one trooper reported that her eyelids “seemed very heavy.”

After claiming that the crash was caused by her car’s “two bad tires,” Dalton agreed to a voluntary drug test. Authorities then confirmed that two substances were detected in her system, which police believe contributed to her crash.

GTA publisher Take-Two projects net bookings (total completed sales, essentially) of $3.35 to $3.5 billion for its current Q3 2027 financial quarter, "driven by the groundbreaking release of Grand Theft Auto 6" in a little over a week.

"The launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is ten days away and, with pre-orders continuing to reach unprecedented levels, we expect to deliver an historic year for our company," said Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick.

The publisher has previously said that it doesn't want to reveal the total number of GTA 6 preorders because "the raw numbers could potentially be misleading," given that it's never seen numbers like these before.

The $3.35 to $3.5 billion net bookings expectation for the GTA 6 launch period is actually slightly below analyst expectations of $3.51 billion, as compiled by LSEG Data & Analytics (via Reuters).

Take-Two's net bookings for its previous financial quarter, Q2 2027, came in below expectations at $1.60 billion, and 18% drop year-over-year. NBA 2K7 was one of the culprits there.

"NBA 2K27 had a successful launch and delivered the second highest Net Bookings performance in the history of the series, but it was below our forecast for the period," said the company.

Zelnick told Bloomberg that he thinks anticipation for GTA 6 contributed to NBA 2K27's lower than expected performance.

#3705. ‘Pride and Prejudice’: See Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden’s Smoldering Take on Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy

It is a truth universally acknowledged that every 10 years or so, we are due for a splashy new version of Pride and Prejudice.

The cycle kicked off some three decades ago, when BBC1 broadcast Andrew Davies’s canonical P&P limited series starring Jennifer Ehle, Colin Firth, and Firth’s wet white shirt—leading to an era of Austenmania that has yet to abate. Ten years later, we got Joe Wright’s instant classic of an adaptation, headlined by Keira Knightley as Elizabeth Bennet and a pre-Succession Matthew Macfadyen as Mr. Darcy. Ten years after that came the regrettable 2016 genre mash-up Pride and Prejudice and Zombies.

Now comes Netflix’s spin on the romantic comedy to end all romantic comedies, starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden as the characters at the center of literature’s original enemies-to-lovers trope.

Sebastian Armesto as Mr. Gardiner, Anjana Vasan as Mrs. Gardiner, and Emma Corrin as Elizabeth Bennet.

But those predecessors weren’t in showrunner Dolly Alderton’s mind as she sat down to craft her interpretation of Jane Austen’s most fiercely adored novel. She instead found inspiration in a less traditional Pride and Prejudice. “The one adaptation that I did reference and I found really useful was Bridget Jones,” says Alderton. Not because her version of Lizzy lip-synchs “All by Myself” or accidentally makes blue soup, but because that 2001 film really understands the character of Wickham—the dashing ne’er-do-well Lizzy is drawn toward before she falls for Darcy.

In the novel, says Alderton, “characters were often talking about how charming he was.” But in her estimation, Austen didn’t spend much time actively showing Wickham’s charm or ease of conversation. “The only examples we really saw of his conversation was him complaining about Darcy, being a bit whingey. I was like, I really need to fool the audience into thinking that he’s the guy that Lizzy should be with.”

Corrin and Matthew Duckett as Colonel Fitzwilliam.

The answer lay in Bridget Jones, which reimagines Wickham as the seductive Daniel Cleaver—Bridget’s bad news boss. As Alderton, a novelist herself, explains, “Cleaver lures Bridget in by making her feel like he’s a safe place to land, to gossip about this person that they both hate”—Colin Firth’s standoffish Mark Darcy. “He’s emulated the language of female intimacy to create a false sense of safety in his company. And there was something of Daniel Cleaver’s mischief and playfulness that plays so opposite against what’s perceived as the stiffness of Darcy that I thought was really useful.” So Alderton infused her Wickham with those qualities. Louis Partridge, who plays the role in the new series, feels like a worthy successor to Hugh Grant.

That case study sums up Alderton’s approach to one of the most frequently adapted works in English literature. Her Pride and Prejudice is both artful and thoughtful, a six-episode series that shows deep respect for its source material while teasing out some of the novel’s less obvious threads—with the help of an uncommonly good cast, some of whom can be seen in character for the first time in these exclusive images. The show’s heart and soul may not actually be Corrin’s Elizabeth or Lowden’s Darcy, but instead the marriage-minded Mrs. Bennet, a character whose overwhelming drive to get her five daughters hitched makes her easy to dismiss.

Daryl McCormack as Mr. Bingley, asking Freya Mavor’s Jane to dance.

When one reads Pride and Prejudice as a teen or a 20-something, it’s easy to get swept up in the romance. If you reread it in your mid-30s, though, you may come to the same realization Alderton did: “Mrs. Bennet’s kind of the hero of the whole fucking thing.” Alderton thinks Elizabeth’s mother has never gotten the credit she deserves: “I really felt I’d like justice for Mrs. Bennet,” she says.

Mrs. Bennet needs to help her daughters find husbands not because she’s in cahoots with the patriarchy or because she’s shallowly obsessed with appearances, but because it’s a critical economic imperative. Alderton wrote a poignant scene in which, during the show’s second episode, Mrs. Bennet explains this to her husband. “This is actually really serious, and you shouldn’t be laughing at me,” the showrunner says, paraphrasing the gist of her speech. “You should be recognizing how much I love my children."

It’s a good monologue, made even better by its delivery from Olivia Colman. The Oscar winner was Alderton’s first and only choice for the role. “I wrote an unbelievably emotional love letter to Olivia, begging her to play Mrs. Bennet, because I knew that our Mrs. Bennet couldn’t be played by anyone else,” the showrunner says. No other actor, she says, has Colman’s ability to “ping-pong, in this really effortless and very genuine way, from very high comedy to very real emotional truth. And that’s really the magic of Austen.”

Siena Kelly and Saffron Coomber as Mr. Bingley’s sisters, Caroline Bingley and Louisa Hurst.

Colman has an ideal foil in Rufus Sewell, who plays Mr. Bennet—a character who, on the page, may seem bemused by his wife at best, and contemptuous of her at worst. Alderton, though, chose to portray their union as one that’s essentially happy. “I think a lot of people think it is an antagonistic marriage,” she says. “But for me, they felt like a very recognizable British couple who are extremely comfortable with each other and deeply fond of each other. And how that deep familiarity is expressed is with relentless mockery, its own expression of love.” After all, she adds, the pair did have five children together in very quick succession—“so I’m sure they liked each other a bit.”

Charming as the elder Bennets may be, every iteration of Pride and Prejudice rests upon the actors who play its central couple. As with Colman, Alderton was certain early on that Corrin and Lowden were the two performers for the job. “Emma can balance that very difficult Lizzy combination of emotional depth and vulnerability and wit and sharpness. Emma’s a very, very, very intelligent person, and I think that’s what you need for Lizzy.”

Lowden, meanwhile, seemed up to the task of playing a notoriously tricky part—a man who seems irredeemably cold and snobbish until Elizabeth visits his estate and discovers how differently Darcy acts when he’s comfortable in his surroundings.

“You have to see a lot of complexity, which means that when we see the real him—when we visit him in Pemberley and we see his gentleness and his loyalty and his protectiveness and his kindness—he doesn’t suddenly feel like a stranger,” Alderton says. “You need a really, really robust actor. You need a really, really muscular actor. That’s what Jack is. And of course, he is also all those things that we need Darcy to be: He’s handsome, he’s sexy, he’s masculine, he’s gallant. So it was a no-brainer, really.”

Is there perhaps another handsome, sexy, masculine, iconically British character she’d like to see him play next? Alderton laughs. “I think my answer is ‘no comment.’”

She’s more open about other things, like the research she did while writing the series—with assists from Professor Fiona Stafford, an Oxford literature professor, and another huge name in Austenland: Emma Thompson, who wrote and starred in Ang Lee’s gold standard adaptation of Sense and Sensibility. When they met before the new Pride and Prejudice started shooting, Thompson gave Alderton some key advice: “You cannot underestimate how important the indicators of class and etiquette are within your scenes. They are so much more than just intricacies of a period drama. They’re a language that signifies some of the most important parts of this time of history.”

There’s strong attention to detail in the final product, every episode of which was directed by Euros Lyn, a veteran of British TV. But there’s also a strong vein of humor—which you’d expect to see from Alderton, whose previous work includes the National Book Award–winning memoir Everything I Know About Love and the best-selling comedic novel Good Material—as well as a sensual current.

Lowden’s Mr. Darcy with his sister Georgiana, played by Isabella Sermon.

It’s too soon for Alderton to pinpoint a sexually charged moment from her series that might enter the vernacular, like Darcy’s wet shirt—“I actually had lunch with Andrew Davies a couple of weeks ago, and I was chastising him for writing that scene: ‘It’s never going to get better than that moment with the wet shirt. It kind of ruined it for all future adapters of Pride and Prejudice’”—or Matthew Macfadyen’s famous hand flex. But the mood is there. “What we’ve ended up with is something that I personally find very erotic,” she says lightly—slightly joking, slightly not.

Adapting a property as beloved as Pride and Prejudice might seem like a daunting prospect. To Alderton, however, it felt practically effortless. Austen’s novel can be seamlessly split into six distinct acts; her dialogue is remarkably lively and speakable, even to modern audiences. “I mean, really she did most of the work for me,” says Alderton. “I just wish she was around to have written screenplays, because she was a really cinematic writer.”

The experience has given Alderton a taste for adaptation—and for tackling narratives with settings that go outside her own personal experience. She’d love to try her hand at William Boyd’s Any Human Heart or Iris Murdoch’s The Sea, the Sea. “I’d love to do an epic. I’d love to write something in wartime. I’d love to write something in the Blitz era.

“I just don’t want to be in 2026 anymore,” Alderton says with a laugh. “I basically want to be in any year other than now. That’s where I want to write my next story.”
