#3574. 10 Best Horror Movie Remakes Of The 21st Century, Ranked

While some folks may still understandably bristle at the idea of horror movies getting the remake treatment, there have been undeniably great ones in recent history. Following celebrated 20th century horror remakes like "Invasion of the Body Snatchers" and "The Thing," the 21st century has its own fair share of memorable chillers. Whether it's Americanized takes on foreign films or updates of longstanding fan-favorites, some of the best horror movies of the 21st century are remakes. With that in mind, we're taking a look at some of the entertaining scary movie remakes released in 2000 and beyond.

A few caveats to keep in mind for this particular list is that remakes that reuse a title but feature a vastly different story, like 2020's excellent "The Invisible Man," are omitted. Other notably enjoyable movies not included here are 2017's "It" and 2013's "Evil Dead," which we would normally recommend but not for the purposes of this list. "It" was previously adapted as a television miniseries, not as a movie, while "Evil Dead" offers a broad retelling, but its post-credits scene suggests it's in the same universe.

All right, here are the 10 best horror movie remakes of the 21st century ranked, each providing a fresh take on an established classic.

There is a surprising number of horror movies set around Valentine's Day, and one of the best horror movies featuring the amorous holiday is the 1981 slasher flick "My Bloody Valentine." This was then remade in 2009 to take advantage of the latest resurgence in 3D filmmaking for American audiences with "My Bloody Valentine 3D." The movie features a small-town community terrorized by a serial killer dressed as a miner linked to a mining tragedy over a decade prior. At the center of this mounting murder mystery is Sheriff Axel Palmer (Kerr Smith) and his old friend Tom Hanniger (Jensen Ackles).

3D gimmickry aside, or maybe partially because of it, "My Bloody Valentine 3D" is a lot of fun. Like its '80s source material, the movie leans into the inherent viciousness of its premise, loading its kills with gratuitous gore and imbuing the character dynamics with heightened melodrama. But the movie also subverts expectations on how this particular version of the story is going to unfold, right down to its climactic confrontation. A deliberately trashy slasher thriller ride, "My Bloody Valentine 3D" hits all the right notes as it retells its tale of small-town carnage.

The 1980 slasher movie "Maniac" is a nasty piece of work, following the perspective of its killer Frank Zito, played by Joe Spinell, who also co-wrote the film. Elijah Wood revisited this concept over 30 years later for the 2012 remake of the same name, starring as Zito. Relocating the gruesome spectacle to Los Angeles, compared to the original's New York City, the remake also unfolds from a first-person perspective. This iteration of Zito also scalps women that encounters, befriending a woman named Anna, played by Nora Arnezeder in the remake, which affects his murderous habit.

With its inventively immersive perspective, the 2012 "Maniac" is one of the most stylishly shot movies on this list. Even with this modern update, the movie doesn't avoid just how sadistic the stakes truly are, with the kills still unrelentingly brutal. Wood really holds the whole thing together, with his wide-eyed performance keeping the audience captivated as he turns lethal on a dime. Bringing a truly twisted take on its already cruel source material, "Maniac" takes slasher bloodletting into an arthouse direction.

This may be a divisive inclusion, given how far it deviates from the original, but some would contend that the 2018 "Suspiria" is the best horror remake ever made. Filmmaker Luca Guadagnino takes the broad premise of the 1977 classic by Dario Argento, with American student Susie Bannion (Dakota Johnson) enrolling in a West German dance academy. As increasingly disturbing and violent phenomena occur around the school, it's revealed that the academy is a front for a coven of witches. This sinister ensemble is headed by Mother Helena Markos (Tilda Swinton), who targets Susie for a fiendish ritual in the inner bowels of the school.

While some argue that the 2018 "Suspiria" remake is better than the original, I won't personally go that far. What I do appreciate is that Guadagnino's version looks and feels markedly different from Argento's film, going with a bleaker color palette and Cold War tension. The movie also does a great job in subverting expectations for those familiar with the original movie, particularly with its sanguine climax. Bringing its own kind of dreary atmosphere rather than Argento's vibrant vision, the 2018 "Suspiria" offers a distinctly entertaining thrill.

Before reimaginings of "Halloween" or "Friday the 13th," it was 2003's "Texas Chainsaw Massacre" that ushered in the slasher remake craze. Directed by Marcus Nispel and produced by Michael Bay, the movie is set in 1973, reflecting its 1974 source material, and it maintains the same basic premise. Protagonist Erin Hardesty (Jessica Biel) is part of a friend group driving through Texas that has a horrific encounter with a hitchhiker. This leads them to the Hewitt family, a cannibalistic clan that includes the masked chainsaw-wielding madman Leatherface (Andrew Bryniarski).

The 2003 "Texas Chainsaw Massacre" brings a slightly more stylish approach to its story, while retaining how mean and nasty the whole thing is. The scariest scenes capitalize on how stealthy Leatherface is, and the remake doubles down on the gore that was only implied in the original. Of all the horror properties remade by Bay's Platinum Dunes, it stands clearly as the best, keeping things hot, tense, and dark as it proceeds. After slashers saw a resurgence with "Scream," "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre" reminded audiences how vicious the genre could be and was all the better for it.

It may have seemed too early to remake the 2022 Dutch-Danish thriller "Speak No Evil" a mere two years later, but the 2024 version quelled all doubts about its efficacy. Written and directed by James Watkins, the remake follows an American family vacationing in Europe who befriend a British family. Accepting an invitation to stay at their remote English home, the Americans grow increasingly uncomfortable with their hosts' behavior. As the ensemble realizes the truth about their devious hosts, they try to escape from their ordeal in one piece.

"Speak No Evil" is an Americanized horror remake that actually works, in contrast to forgettable fare like "Pulse" or "The Uninvited." A big part of that success is Watkins not slavishly sticking to the source material, while staying true to the spirit of the original version. James McAvoy, playing the duplicitous host masterminding this getaway from hell is in fine form as always, having previously proved his horror bonafides in "Split." Considerably less bleak than the original version, the "Speak No Evil" remake doesn't compromise its brutal stakes as it offers its own take on the story.

Looking back, Zack Snyder's best film is his 2004 "Dawn of the Dead" remake, and it's not even close. Whereas the 1978 original by George A. Romero took place with the zombie apocalypse underway, the remake opens with the start of undead ravenously rising. This brutally intense beginning sets the tone for the rest of the movie, complete with zombies that chase down their prey at a full sprint. Like the original, the movie centers on a small group of survivors who take shelter in a shopping mall, barricading themselves from the undead amassing outside.

The 2004 "Dawn of the Dead" takes its scares seriously, though it does offer its own moments of dark humor with a larger ensemble of main characters. Snyder brings a saturated cinematography to the action, giving the movie a striking visual style that sets it apart from the original and reflects its contemporary aesthetics. But this all takes a backseat to how pulse-poundingly intense the whole ride is, starting and ending particularly strong. The "Dawn of the Dead" remake feels tougher and meaner than Romero's original, setting the stage for "The Walking Dead" to unleash a resurgence in zombie fiction.

Before "The Lost Boys," there was "Fright Night" as a classic '80s teen vampire flick that gave audiences a bloody good time. The 1985 movie received a remake by Disney, of all studios, in 2011, retelling the story of geeky teenager Charley Brewster (Anton Yelchin) getting a vampire as a nextdoor neighbor. This charming bloodsucker, Jerry (Colin Farrell), realizes Charley has learned his secret and targets the teen as he turns more and more members of the community into his undead ranks. Desperate, Charley recruits Las Vegas magician Peter Vincent (David Tennant) to help him vanquish the vampire and save his victims.

While it doesn't have the same campy charm as the 1985 original, the 2011 "Fright Night" is a surprisingly good remake. A lot of this comes from the strength of its main cast, including Yelchin, Tennant, and Imogen Poots as Charley's love interest Amy Peterson. But the real standout is Colin Farrell as an all-time great horror villain, both smolderingly sexy and bringing plenty of monstrous menace. Smartly constructed and repurposed to appeal to modern audiences, the "Fright Night" remake is a solidly sanguine take on the story.

The 1998 Japanese horror movie "Ringu" was remade for American audiences as "The Ring" in 2002 by a pre "Pirates of the Caribbean" Gore Verbinski. The movie follows journalist Rachel Keller (Naomi Watts) who learns about a cursed video tape that mysteriously kills anyone who watches it seven days after a viewing. When both Rachel and her young son Aidan (David Dorfman) watch the tape, they have to find a way to be spared of the curse before it's too late. This leads Rachel to launch an exhaustive investigation into the history of the tape and the haunting figure who appears in its footage.

Over 20 years after debut, "The Ring" has evolved into a horror masterpiece that's arguably better than its Japanese source material. Verbinski's American version handles its dramatic scenes more effectively, and Watts is phenomenal in her lead performance. The 2002 movie also provides its own terrifying scares and explores the moral consequences of escaping the central curse on a deeper level than Hideo Nakata's original. Starting a wave of American remakes of Japanese horror movies, none did this cultural transposition better than "The Ring."

Before he helmed "The Batman," filmmaker Matt Reeves crafted his own version of the Swedish horror movie "Let the Right One In." Retitled "Let Me In," the 2010 movie offers its own retelling of Owen (Kodi Smit-McPhee), an ostracized boy in 1983 New Mexico, befriending a vampire. After meeting Abby (Chloë Grace Moretz), Owen realizes that she's a vampire, but he quickly forges a friendship with her that develops into something more. This young romance is challenged by the community discovering Abby's growing body count, while Owen's bullies escalate their harassment.

Though it retains the narrative broad strokes, Matt Reeves avoids making a copy-paste remake with "Let Me In." To really distinguish his version, Reeves leans into the aesthetics and sensibilities of Reagan-era America, complete with a memorable television broadcast by Reagan himself. That added cultural context goes a long way in imbuing the 2010 movie with its own personality, while still bringing plenty of vampiric action. Punctuating its coming-of-age romance with gruesome scares, "Let Me In" respects its source material while making its tale distinctly American.

In remaking the 1922 silent film masterpiece "Nosferatu," filmmaker Robert Eggers dug up his lifelong love of vampires for his 2024 version. The movie reframes Ellen Hutter (Lily-Rose Depp) as someone targeted by the vampiric Count Orlok (Bill Skarsgård) since she was a little girl in 19th century Germany. Years later, Ellen's husband Thomas (Nicholas Hoult) meets Orlok at his Transylvanian home to sell him property in his hometown before learning his client is a vampire. Orlok brings death and pestilence with him to Germany, prompting Ellen to resort to desperate means to save her community from this undead terror.

Robert Eggers resurrects "Nosferatu" as a scary fever dream, significantly dialing up the sensual themes to the story. This approach is underscored and elevated by Eggers' penchant for striking art design, with the 2024 remake being his most visually sumptuous production to date. While everyone in the cast does a stellar job, including Depp and Skarsgård, it's Eggers' usual collaborator Willem Dafoe who steals every scene that he's in. Remaking "Nosferatu" is always a tall order, but Eggers proved himself more than ready for the task, while including his usual themes into this retelling.

#3573. Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s Coolest Dungeon Hides a Secret Tribute to a Beloved Classic

Nintendo's highly anticipated remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is finally here, and millions of players are reliving their childhood adventures or experiencing Link's journey for the very first time. Though the Nintendo 64 game has received a dramatic visual glow-up for the Switch 2, the remake meticulously preserves the spirit of the original — including an extended reference to a classic American novel that even Ocarina diehards may have missed the first time around.

[Ed. note: Mid-game spoilers ahead for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. If you haven't retrieved the Master Sword yet, turn back now!]

After Link collects the three Spiritual Stones and returns to Hyrule Castle Town to claim the Master Sword, we move forward seven years in time. Link is now an adult, and in order to thwart Ganon's terrifying reign, he must awaken six sages throughout Hyrule by visiting their temples and claiming their power for his own. The first of these is located just outside Link's hometown of Kokiri Village, land of the fairy folk. Though most of his youthful pals don't recognize the grown-up Link, they urge him to investigate the Forest Temple and rescue their dear friend Saria.

When Link ventures into the Forest Temple, he discovers something altogether unexpected: an eerie, luxurious old mansion inhabited by ghosts. As he enters a central room flanked by colorful torches, four ghostly Poes appear to snatch away the flames. Venturing deeper into the mansion, Link discovers that these ghoulish gals are actually four sisters: Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy.

Sound familiar? Those are the same names (and the same birth order) as the March sisters in Louisa May Alcott's novel Little Women. It's a timeless coming-of-age story about four sisters who have very different goals and ambitions in life, one that's been adapted countless times for stage and screen. The most recent adaptation is the 2019 film by Barbie and The Magician's Nephew director Greta Gerwig, which stars Saoirse Ronan, Florence Pugh, and Timothée Chalamet.

While you might be inclined to think this is some newfangled meddling with the localization, these were also the Poe Sisters' names in the Nintendo 64 original. (There's one exception: the second sister, Jo, was called "Joelle" in the 1998 game.) Naturally, there are plenty of "well actually" guys pointing this out in the comments of social media posts. But it's still a fun little Easter egg for players discovering it for the first time, whether or not they've played Ocarina of Time before.

If you're like me and have never played Ocarina of Time until now, be sure to check out Polygon's extensive guides and walkthroughs for the remake. Like this hidden node, there are plenty of puzzle solutions, hidden items, and valuable power-ups you can easily miss on your first playthrough.

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

#3572. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3571. Dolly Parton Is Gone, But Dollywood Will Always Love Her

“RIP Dolly Smoky Mountain Angel” was one of the first signs we saw as we pulled up on the side of a motel in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. Just down the same road was another memorial to her on a Burger King sign. This was in early October. Dolly Parton, the country singer and actor, widely considered a Great American Who Everyone Loves, had died, at the age of 80, in late August. I am not the kind of person who cries over celebrity deaths, but after I heard that she died, I went to my closet to find a Dolly Parton T-shirt I had bought the one time I saw her live, at a concert of mostly acoustic songs in Queens in 2016. I couldn’t find it. I blamed my brief flirtation with the Marie Kondo method, but there was no way that T-shirt hadn’t sparked joy.

Early October in Sevier County, in far eastern Tennessee, where Parton was born, is full of cabins on some parcels of land that dot the ancient Appalachians. But among the rolling green expanses are Mexican supermarkets, coffee shops, apple orchards, and pumpkin patches. This is where she opened the amusement park Dollywood in 1986. The Great Smoky Mountains National Park draws masses about 13 miles from Dollywood. The fancier of my friends identified the area as where the Blackberry Farm resort is. But Pigeon Forge has a feeling of a Jersey Shore boardwalk in Appalachia, with a strip of businesses that sell vapes and ATV rides and Moon Pies a block from a Margaritaville hotel.

Parton opened Dollywood in 1986 at the foothills of the Great Smoky Mountains. Today, it draws in millions of people annually—loving fans who don her iconic pink cowboy hat or accessories honoring the park's famous Grist Mill Cinnamon Bread (a cult favorite).

Locals heap the kind of praise on Parton that we’ve come to expect knowing her reputation as a goddess among mortals. “People don’t understand what she did for this place and meant to this place. She threw lots of money at it and went out of her way to take care of this place,” an Uber driver named Eric told me as we exited the highway into Dollywood, with its script logo and “love every moment” greeting signs. “I got to meet her three times at the park because she would just show up and stand there with a crowd of people. For someone who’s been famous as long as she’s been famous you’d expect a certain air of haughtiness,” he says. “But I was stunned at how kind she was.”

Parton’s job title at the park was dreamer-in-chief, and part of Dollywood’s allure is that it’s a shrine to her life and career. There’s a replica of the two-room wood cabin where she grew up a sharecropper’s daughter, in close quarters alongside her parents and 10 siblings. Her home, not even 500 square feet, had no electricity nor running water. (The original home still stands about 10 miles away but isn’t open to the public.)

Parton wrote the country ballad “I Will Always Love You” in 1973 as a heartfelt farewell to her longtime business partner Porter Wagoner. Now, fans honoring Dolly's memory have used the slogan for the park's new annual festival, which opens in March 2027.

That modest beginning is plenty known, but Dollywood also celebrates Parton as she became a household name and wildly rich. The Dolly Parton Experience is a museum devoted to her trajectory, from Nashville ingenue to a celebrity among celebrities (photos show her with Mick Jagger in the ’60s and Whitney Houston in the ’90s). It has a gallery devoted to her Imagination Library, which has donated more than 300 million books to children around the world. Another building across a landscaped path celebrates her role in the workplace revenge comedy 9 to 5 (September 25 has now been christened a holiday in Sevier County) and houses a half dozen of her wigs, sorted by decade, all platinum, all voluminous. A plaque commemorates her wig stylists, starting with her Aunt Colleen. Parton’s costumes are scattered around the tributes, including a black flared jumpsuit with a hot pink shirt and neck ruffle so intense it looks Elizabethan. One wall features one of Parton’s famously self-effacing quotes: “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap.”

In her mobile home, which guests line up around to take a tour, she has a closet with a hanging yellow diamanté dress, a full-size bathtub because she preferred baths to showers, mirrored ceilings because she was claustrophobic, and cheeky digital clocks that display her most hallowed time zones: Dollywood (5:53 p.m. ET) and Nashville (4:53 p.m. CT). I ask our tour guide, a woman in a sparkly vest, how she and the park employees have fared without Parton. “Today is the first day I haven’t cried,” she admits.

Dollywood is more than a museum—it's an amusement park. The 165-acre Pigeon Forge carnival features over 50 rides and Dollywood's Splash Country, a 35-acre water park.

But more than a museum, Dollywood is an amusement park, and a much bigger one than I had realized. It’s a place where you can stand in line for 45 minutes to buy a corn dog while listening to a four-person singing-and-dancing group in the vein of the Mickey Mouse Club does peppy but half-assed covers of Fleetwood Mac and Van Halen. Looping rollercoasters and water tube rides leave families soaking wet in matching T-shirts commemorating their vacations. Dondre, my colleague and our photographer for this journey, waits probably a full hour to squeeze into a vintage muscle car with me so I can simulate steering around a track. It wasn’t until deep into our wait time that we realize this is a children’s ride. At this point, the two of us notice that, in the sea of people, we are the only ones who are childless, wearing dark colors, and audibly bemoaning that Dollywood is dry. (Parton was not a strict teetotaler, but the park bills itself as assertively family-friendly. “Weapons and alcoholic beverages are not permitted on Dollywood Property” is the only explanation given on its website.) No one else seems to care. The ride is quick, but we are ecstatic, high on refillable Diet Cokes, kettle corn, and driving a car, which neither one of us knows how to do in real life.

Some park employees have not fared well without Parton. One tour guide admits: “Today is the first day I haven’t cried." Parton passed away on August 25 at the age of 80 after a battle with cancer.

We don’t want real life at Dollywood. We want the dreamer-in-chief’s dreams. For dinner, we hit the 8:30 show of Dolly Parton’s Stampede in Pigeon Forge, an equestrian version of dinner theater where guests are served a whole chicken, pulled pork, corn, greens, a biscuit, pie, and unlimited soda, all to be eaten by hand while the not so vague perfume of manure wafts through the air. Horses with cowboys and cowgirls astride them jump through rings of fire, someone does wire work while dangling from the ceiling, and American flags fly in abundance. We catch a pig race. Sooo-ey! At another point, a volunteer from the audience disappears from a barrel before our eyes. The whole thing feels psychedelic, and we peak when performers in butterfly wings ride around to Parton’s song “Love Is Like a Butterfly.” I squeal as a few actual buffalo take the arena. After the show, I ask a cowboy how the majestic creatures are as animal coworkers, and he shakes his head. “There’s a reason I stick to horses.”

Even in the perfect bubble of Dollywood, in the wake of her death, Parton’s spirit has already faded into the nostalgia.

There isn’t enough acknowledgement of Parton’s death at the park for my taste; no candlelit vigil or impersonators we can hug. By the second day, my mania has subsided, giving way to contemplation. I ask fellow parkgoers if they have come to pay respects. Every single one replies that their trip has been planned long before. My attempts to make small talk with strangers doesn’t result in the fantasy of one collective mourning. Families in seasonal T-shirts seem shy and uninterested in chatting with me, a strangely inquisitive middle-aged woman who wants to ask them if they’ve heard the rumor that Dolly Parton was secretly covered in tattoos. (They haven’t.) A friend group of two lesbian couples from Pennsylvania brushes off my line of questioning around whether Parton might have been more than just queer-friendly (rainbow Dollywood shirts and backpacks and trucker caps are for sale). Too soon, they say, and shake their heads—too salacious to be airing gossip. I ask other strangers if they have heard the family drama over Parton’s estate. Most dismiss me, but another Uber driver, this one named Austin, says, “She has a huge estate and a big family, and it was always going to happen. We’ll see how it plays out.” (In November, the lawsuit was dropped, and Parton’s nephew said he was happy to put the issue behind him.)

The butterfly is a key part of Dollywood's logo, representing Parton's personal emblem. As a little girl growing up in the Smoky Mountains, she was fascinated by butterflies and related to their gentle grace. She cemented the motif into her career in 1974 with the hit song, “Love is Like a Butterfly.”

Maybe, I say to Dondre, no one will talk to me because I, unlike about 50% of the people there, am not wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with a Bible verse, a military slogan, or a celebration of America’s 250 years. I keep pointing out paintings of crosses and eagles and American flags—often all combined on one canvas together—for sale. Dondre says, in a kind way, that nothing is more cliché than hearing someone from New York talk about other parts of the country. Maybe what made Dolly Parton so winning—her apparent lack of judgment—is not something I inherently have. It can’t hurt to try to be a little more like Parton in our own daily lives.

Maybe she had an optimism no one can ever replace. And that’s ultimately okay because you can try to channel that anywhere. Even in the perfect bubble of Dollywood, in the wake of her death, Parton’s spirit has already faded into the nostalgia, a curio like Graceland, but with a vintage steam train ride.

I succumb and buy a Christmas ornament with Parton dressed as Santa and eat a chicken salad sandwich served on a butterfly-logo-shaped pretzel. I guess I enjoy Dollywood the way I enjoy going dancing in Berlin gay clubs or karaoke birthday parties: It is an experience, and a fun one, but not what I would choose. I will never, in the vein of a Disney Adult, be a Dolly Adult. More power to those who cherish their season passes. But Parton doesn’t even have to be core to your identity for you to enjoy an intricately branded amusement park. Its unchanging presence is a comfort. If you need to commune with her earthly treasures, there is always Dollywood. May her costumes and wigs remain.

Dollywood will always be a place for fans and dreamers alike to marvel in the wonder of the country icon’s extraordinary career and charming home.

#3570. Before Batman: The Killing Joke, Legendary Comic Writer Alan Moore Wrote A Clayface Story

Ah, the 1980s, when a not-yet-broken-by-the-comics-industry Alan Moore would still write as work for hire on superhero comics. In 1986, Moore wrote "Whatever Happened To The Man of Tomorrow?" and imagined a hypothetical ending for the Superman mythos.

The previous year, Moore contributed three Richard Corben-drawn pages to the exquisite corpse comic "Heroes for Hope: Starring the X-Men." Moore depicts the then-reformed Magneto experiencing a bleak fantasy of a ruined world where his Brotherhood of Evil Mutants stands triumphant, albeit on a mountain of corpses.

Then there's 1988's "The Killing Joke," the infamous origin (maybe) for the Joker. It's one of the most famous and influential Batman stories ever. "Batman" and "Batman Returns" director Tim Burton has said, "['The Killing Joke' is] the first comic I've ever loved." But many hate it for a pivotal sequence where the Joker shoots, strips, and disables Barbara Gordon.

Moore has praised Brian Bolland's artwork but has voiced regrets about writing the comic. "I think ['The Killing Joke'] put far too much melodramatic weight upon a character that was never designed to carry it. It was too nasty, it was too physically violent," Moore has said, feeling it spawned the "regrettable trend" of "grimness and psychosis" in superhero comics.

Previously, in 1987, Moore wrote a story about a different Batman villain: Clayface. "Mortal Clay," drawn by artist George Freeman, was published in "Batman Annual" #11. The issue (advertised as "Villains In Love!") includes two stories: "Love Bird," a backup by Max Allan Collins and Norm Breyfogle, about the Penguin attempting to reform, and "Mortal Clay," about Clayface's obsessive romance with ... a department store mannequin. It's got the flowery prose and super-villainous psychological depth of "The Killing Joke" without the "nastiness" that makes that story a classic in most people's eyes (but not Moore's).

"Mortal Clay" is not about Matt Hagen, the character featured in the DC Universe's "Clayface" movie (played by Tom Rhys Harries). In the "Batman" comics, there have been many Clayfaces. "Mortal Clay" is about the third one, Preston Payne, who's distinguished by his wearing a glass helmet containment suit.

Clayface III debuted in "Detective Comics" #478-479 by Len Wein and Marshall Rogers. Preston Payne had the hormone disorder acromegaly. To cure his condition, he stole a sample of Matt Hagen's blood, hoping Clayface's shapeshifting would transfer over to him. Instead, he not only became a mud monster like Hagen but one with a touch that dissolves living flesh (hence his containment suit).

Payne is also delusional. He dotes on his girlfriend, Helena, even rushing back into his burning hideout to save her. Except "Helena" is actually a wax museum figurine, because Payne can only touch inanimate matter. During these issues, Batman is reeling from his girlfriend Silver St. Cloud leaving him, so a romantic villain makes for a compelling foil.

Clayface's dark romantic spirit carries over into "Mortal Clay." Searching Gotham City, Clayface rediscovers "Helena" (really, a department store mannequin). He embraces her like a lover and hides himself in the mall so at night, he and Helena can "live" as man and wife.

"Mortal Clay" is narrated entirely by Preston, with a clear dissonance between what his warped mind claims and what the more objective images of the comic show. Later in his narration, he claims men close their eyes when they kiss because they're afraid they won't see love in their partner's eyes staring back. Maybe that's one reason why men like Preston prefer a "woman" who is literally just a pretty object, incapable of speech or thought.

"Mortal Clay" explores the loneliness that Clayface's poisonous touch brings. Payne embraces his delusions because that's the only "love" possible for him. The way Clayface anthropomorphizes Helena, though, leads to jealousy and ruin. He thinks Helena is "cheating" on him when she's used as a lingerie standee, or when a night guard steals a scarf off her display for his own wife — cue Clayface melting him. Once Batman shows up to investigate the murder, Payne concludes the Dark Knight is Helena's gentleman caller. Batman, for his part, recognizes what's happening and pleads: "Preston ... let me help."

"Mortal Clay" ends with Clayface sitting in Arkham Asylum with Helena. Payne drinks beer, watches TV, and resents his "wife" — a portrait of a marriage. In a closing line of beautiful dramatic irony, Payne smirks and narrates: "One day I shall be free [of Helena]. After all, she can't live forever."

"The Killing Joke" also ends with Batman extending his hand and offering to help a nemesis. The Joker rejects it, not spitefully but earnestly, because "The Killing Joke" demonstrates Alan Moore's belief there has to be something human that drives the Joker. ("Dark Knight Returns" author Frank Miller, who feels the Joker is "evil incarnate," claims he and Moore once had an hours-long disagreement about that.)

The best companion piece for "Mortal Clay," though, is Moore and Rick Veitch's "Swamp Thing" #56, or "My Blue Heaven." Stranded on an alien world, Swamp Thing uses his powers to remake a simulacrum of his life on Earth, including a plant puppet of his wife Abby. But Swamp Thing knows he's fooling himself, whereas Clayface deludes himself into genuinely believing Helena is a real person. As "Mortal Clay" shows, not even that ignorance has brought him bliss.

#3568. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3567. Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries Face Democratic Leadership Revolt After Midterms

The latest conflict brewing in the Democratic Party’s cold war between the blue dogs and the insurgent progressive wing is the fight over its next congressional leaders. But with no alternate candidates stepping up to run, it’s hard to determine how real the threats to replace Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries actually are.

At least six incoming Democratic senators—including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan, Illinois’s Juliana Stratton, Kansas’s Adam Hamilton, and Maine’s Troy Jackson—have said they won’t support Schumer for majority leader. Michigan senator Elissa Slotkin has called for a “a new generation of leadership.” Even Cory Booker, who praised Schumer for helping engineer last week’s blue wave, stopped short of saying whether he would support him. On Monday, Richard Blumenthal did the same. And Jon Stewart said that the senator “does not understand the urgency of the moment and what the future demands.” Regardless, Schumer is confident. His aides say he has enough votes to become the next majority leader.

In the House, several incoming Democrats—including Claire Valdez, Angela Gonzalez-Torres, Darializa Avila Chevalier, Melat Kiros, Adam Hamawy, Chris Rabb, and Donavan McKinney—have been noncommittal with their support for Jeffries, while Ohio democrat Don Leonard has threatened to seek alternative leadership unless Jeffries changes his position on Israel.

There’s an online effort to prevent Jeffries from becoming Speaker of the House. A change.org petition demanding that House Democrats reject Jeffries as their next Speaker has attracted more than 1 million signatures as of Sunday, with actor Mark Ruffalo among those encouraging people to sign. But scroll to the bottom of the petition, and you’ll find a disclosure: Its creator, Nicole Whitted, is a paid “Change Ambassador” who receives compensation from change.org in connection with the signatures. “Thousands of organizations and brands worldwide run similar programs and in the social-cause space specifically, it’s a way to encourage people with reach and influence to use their voice for causes they care about,” Whitted told Vanity Fair in a statement.

Whitted also said she was traveling to Washington, DC next week to urge congresspeople to vote against Jeffries, and to meet with Representative Ayanna Pressley, whom Whitted told VF she’ll be supporting for Speaker. Pressley’s team did not respond to Vanity Fair’s request for comment sent on Sunday. Neither did her closest congressional allies, Rashida Tlaib, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, or Ilhan Omar.

Reports indicate that some congresspeople have been flooded with calls from constituents urging them to find new party leadership. But one Democratic aide told Vanity Fair that they’ve noticed what they claim is a coordinated effort to undermine Jeffries on social media, including AI-generated videos attacking Jeffries that have gotten tens of thousands of engagements.

The Brooklyn congressman does have good relationships with members of both the moderate “blue dogs” and the party’s progressive flank. Ocasio-Cortez has already backed him, and last month, Representative Ro Khanna declared that “Hakeem Jeffries is going to be Speaker.” “Don’t believe what you’re seeing on the internet,” the aide said. “It’s not reality.”

Schumer’s allies, meanwhile, have been reminding skeptics of the work he did to deliver the Democratic majority. The New York senator helped recruit candidates including Roy Cooper and Sherrod Brown, while the Democratic political operation supporting Senate candidates spent lavishly on competitive races. According to final figures provided to Vanity Fair, Senate Majority PAC and its affiliates spent nearly $407 million across races in eight states, including $150 million in Ohio, $67 million apiece in Iowa and Michigan, $65 million in Maine, and $40 million in Texas, all of which flipped. Another $14 million went toward Kansas, with smaller investments in Mississippi and South Carolina—$2.2 million and $750,000 respectively. Some of that money helped elect candidates who are now skeptical about whether Schumer should stay in charge.

In the House, each party will choose its leadership this month, but in order to become Speaker, a candidate still needs to get a majority of the entire chamber, usually 218 members, to vote for them when the new Congress convenes in January. It’s a little easier in the Senate, where the Democrat will only need to win a simple majority of their own caucus in an anonymous early December vote to become majority leader.

El-Sayed has suggested Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen, although a source close to Van Hollen told Vanity Fair that he isn’t planning to run, instead setting his sights on a potential presidential campaign in 2028. “Prior to selecting a majority leader, Senator Van Hollen believes the caucus needs to have an honest and open conversation about how we move an agenda forward that reflects the will of the American people,” says a Democratic aide familiar with the senator’s thinking. “He’s made clear that Democrats need to use their power to immediately end the illegal war with Iran, advance a robust pro-worker kitchen table agenda, and fight political corruption.”

Another name circulating among Democratic aides is Hawaii senator Brian Schatz, a relatively young progressive who has developed relationships across the party’s ideological factions and is already pursuing the number-two leadership position being vacated by retiring senator Dick Durbin.

“He’s the heir apparent,” one Democratic aide told Vanity Fair, describing Schatz as someone who could appeal to both progressives and moderates. Asked about speculation surrounding his leadership ambitions, Schatz’s spokesperson offered a noncommittal response: “I don’t have anything new to share on this but will keep you posted if that changes.”

Some Democrats are also hesitant to replace their experienced leaders after they’ve been given this narrow opportunity to get stuff done with control of both chambers of Congress. “I don’t think you’d want somebody new who’s, like, learning the ropes while we have the opportunity to really get meaningful legislation passed for the American people,” another Democratic aide said.

Still, the fighting online and on cable news exposes a tension within the Democratic Party. Moderates see the blue wave as vindication of the party’s disciplined, affordability-focused strategy. Progressives see it as a mandate for a more ambitious agenda—and a rejection of the establishment’s familiar faces.

Both factions are claiming the election as their own victory. But before they can fight over what to do with their new power, they’ll have to decide who’s going to lead them.

#3566. How to get the Golden Scale in Zelda Ocarina of Time

The Golden Scale is a unique item in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake that allows Link to dive deeper. You can consider it an upgrade to the Silver Scale, an item that you obtain as young Link as you try to find Princess Ruto. However, unlike the Silver Scale, you can only get the Golden Scale after becoming adult Link.

If you would like to explore the depths of Hyrule and hunt for all the treasures hidden underwater, you should learn how to get the Golden Scale in the Ocarina of Time remake.

You obtain the Golden Scale by catching a fish longer than 60 cm in the Fishing Pond. To complete the challenge, you must travel south of Hyrule Field to Lake Hylia as adult Link. You will see that the lake is dry, and you won't be able to reach the Fishing Pond, located on the right side of the map, on your own. You will need to either ride a magic bean plant (that you need to plant as child Link next to the laboratory) or play the Scarecrow Song near the bridge at the front of the building, and then use the Hookshot on to it. Lake Hylia will also be refilled once you clear the Water Temple, so you can come back after that, too.

Once inside, talk to the Fishing-Pond Man and learn that you can earn a prize if "you catch a big enough fish." Rent a fishing rod for 30 rupees, allowing you to fish as many times as you want until you tell the Fishing-Pond Man that you're done. When preparing to cast your bait, we suggest that you aim at the middle of the pond where you can usually find big fish.

Big fish are more difficult to reel in because they resist for longer periods. Just be patient and keep moving the rod in the direction the fish is pulling. If you catch a fish that is smaller than 60 cm, you just need to toss it back and keep trying until you find the right fish.

However, if you get a fish that meets the requirements, keep it, and then go talk to the Fishing-Pond Man. Select the "I'm done" option and he will examine your fish, and you will receive the Golden Scale.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

#3565. DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn And Peter Safran Out, Marvel Veteran Jeremy Latcham Taking Over

Today brings the stunning end of an era for DC Studios — yes, another one. Only four years after James Gunn and Peter Safran were brought on board to shepherd a rebooted DC Universe on the big and small screens, both creative heads are officially out and former Marvel Cinematic Universe creative Jeremy Latcham is in as their replacement. The news comes straight from the top of the newly-merged Skydance corporation, which has taken over ownership of the DC franchise following its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. In an official release, Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz had this to say:

"James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we're incredibly proud of. We're grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand."

"Shocking" doesn't even begin to cover this turn of events, which comes only weeks after Gunn and Safran indicated Ellison appeared to be in favor of keeping both on board following the studio merger (via The Hollywood Reporter). Obviously, things have changed quite dramatically since then, with Ellison now pivoting to new leadership. Latcham may be familiar to Marvel fans as the former executive who produced several early films in the Marvel Cinematic Universe under Kevin Feige's leadership. Now, he'll get his chance at the top job as the newly-installed President and Chief Creative Officer of DC Studios ... even as several questions remain unanswered.

If it seems like the only consistency over at DC has been inconsistency over the last several years, you're not wrong! Ever since Zack Snyder was installed as the creative lead with "Man of Steel" in 2013, Marvel's distinguished competition has been beset by creative shakeups and overhauls ever since. Snyder gave way to a revolving door of several individual directors adding onto the then-DC Extended Universe, a brief (and bizarre) fling with Dwayne Johnson, an Elseworlds pivot with Todd Phillips' two "Joker" films and Matt Reeves' "The Batman," and most recently James Gunn and Peter Safran's unified take on the DC Universe.

Now, ex-Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham will be the next one on the hot seat ... and, at this point, it's unclear if DC will now undergo yet another top-to-bottom reboot under Skydance. That would be more than a bit awkward with Gunn's "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow" still slated to release next year, more DC movies to come afterwards, and even multiple shows currently in development (including a "Poison Ivy"-focused series). Could Latcham simply guide the next batch of movies and shows to come, keeping everything in a loose continuity with the foundation Gunn and Safran established? The biggest hint might be found in the joint statement by David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz:

"Jeremy has been a longtime creative partner to both, and we have complete confidence that James and Peter will ensure a smooth, collaborative transition and continue this work with care. We look forward to working with Jeremy to build the next generation of DC storytelling and to doubling down on our commitment to fans."

Stay tuned to /FIlm as we wait and see how Latcham's DC will ultimately take shape.

#3564. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

Pixar movies have been entertaining audiences for decades, especially the Toy Story franchise. We were treated to another adventure with everyone's favorite toys when Toy Story 5 hit theaters earlier this year, with the project now streaming with a Disney+ subscription. I've been wondering why that army of Buzz Lightyears spent so much of the film wandering around the woods, and now we finally have some answers behind that narrative choice.

Toy Story 5 reviews were positive, and plenty of folks liked the running gag of all the Buzz Lightyears roaming around the woods together. During an interview with Gold Derby, director/writer Andrew Stanton got real about why the squad of Buzz toys spent so much time in the wilderness. As he explained:

We wanted them in the woods because then they wouldn't be constantly bumping into humans. And we just needed a nondescript shortcut to get wherever they're going. But then somebody in my story group drew a Buzz Lightyear petting a bunny, and it was like watching an actor choose something that was instinctual. We all knew that deep down under that tough exterior that Buzz has such a soft heart. And animals can sense when you're kind. And it just made sense that they would get along with cute woodland creatures.

Honestly, this makes a great deal of sense. We all know that toys in the animated franchise play dead whenever humans encounter them, hiding the secret that they're actually alive. So when Toy Story 5 brought in an entire group of new Buzz Lightyears, they had to be put in a setting that allowed the action figures to continue guarding that secret.

Toy Story 5 made fans appreciate Jessie, but the running gag of all the Buzz Lightyears was a delightful side plot during the movie's 102-minute runtime. It was heartwarming to see the toys connecting with various animals in the woods, which also served as an A+ reference to Bambi. As the filmmaker went on to share:

And there's something meta about woodland creatures and animation and Bambi, and it just felt like all these roads met at the same time to the degree that when we were putting the scene together and it was cracking us up privately by putting Bambi's ['Love Is a Song'] in there. I said we should look into getting the rights because it's the one time I would be willing to go off script composer-wise, much to Randy Newman's chagrin. But to really sell the joke and to sell the moment, it's just this kind of animation history.

The Toy Story franchise is known for including easter eggs to other Disney projects, so the fact that the fifth movie went full Bambi shouldn't have come as much of surprise. Still, I'm glad that we got some answers about why the Buzz squad was kept in the woods for the majority of the movie.

Toy Story 5 is streaming now on Disney+ as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll just have to see if the House of Mouse moves forward with a sixth installment of the beloved property.

#3562. Elon Musk’s Cybertruck Is Dumb, Ugly, and Mercifully Dead

In March 2024, a Tesla Cybertruck speeding down Sunset Boulevard slammed head-on into the Beverly Hills Hotel’s iconic entrance sign just before midnight. Passersby winding through the Flats slowed down to watch as Elon Musk’s statue to his own insecurities—the stainless steel embodiment of nuance-free American ego—demolished in front of Hollywood’s unofficial canteen.

Every decade gets the iconography it deserves. At just about the midpoint of the 2020s, ours had arrived, fully formed.

And now the Cybertruck is dead, which is wonderful news. Musk, who’s having a historically bad November, announced late last week that Tesla will be “winding down” production of the Cybertruck around mid-2027, putting an end to the most hated car in America. I was going to call it the most polarizing car in America, but honestly, no one likes this thing. And it’s not entirely due to anti-Elon sentiment: Tesla’s general sales have been relatively steady, going down a bit as Musk went full DOGE mode in 2025 before rebounding in 2026. People like Elon’s cars. They just do not like the Cybertruck.

True, its death has been mourned by some—especially the self-selecting devotees who installed bulletproof glass in their Cybertrucks before shooting them with rifles. These people exist. But mostly, the news has been greeted with a rush of enthusiasm, relief, and, more than anything else, blue-pilled schadenfreude.

Now would be the right moment in the news cycle for an art writer such as myself to make a contrarian argument: that the Cybertruck was secretly a design masterpiece—some kind of neo-Donald Judd breakthrough unleashed ahead of its time.

I am not going to make that argument, because that is not true. Not even close. No one in the future will look back on the Cybertruck as an unheralded art object. It’s The Jetsons for meatheads, a Batmobile for people who secretly root for the Joker. It looks like a birdhouse designed by Zaha Hadid, which I would love to have as a vessel for feeding hungry birds at my (sadly hypothetical) Zaha Hadid house. But I would not want it as a vehicle to park in a driveway. It is a bad car.

And yet, that crashed Cybertruck in front of the Beverly Hills Hotel is seared into my brain, playing on repeat like the most un-subtle Lana Del Rey song ever written. Even beyond that crash, the Cybertruck is the ultimate symbol of this surreal and cruel decade, one that started with a global pandemic and a government suggesting the possibility of a bleach injection as treatment. It’s a decade that wound through four years of a former president denying the lawful election of a current president, only to see that former president return to power. Through it all, we’ve sunk deeper into our collective psychosis—one that’s forced us into rooms with our devices, addicted to social media and artificial intelligence, consuming half-real information and spewing it back out into the world.

It’s a perfect world for the Tesla Cybertruck to define.

The Cybertruck arrived right at the dawn of the decade, in what we can now see as a completely different timeline.

Musk unveiled the car in November 2019 at Tesla’s design studio. Head designer Franz von Holzhausen attempted to demonstrate the vehicle’s shatterproof glass by hurtling a metal ball at a window at full speed. The window shattered. Great omen! It was also pretty weird that Musk was introduced by a hologram of someone called “Cybergirl,” who people speculated was actually a hologram of Grimes, the pop star Musk was dating at the time.

Plenty of design press fawned over the shiny new thing—“Long live the Cybertruck. See you in the Thunderdome,” wrote Dwell. But Wired wisely asked the opinion of an actual expert: Raphael Zammit, who chairs automobile design at Motor City’s own College for Creative Studies.

“I was like, ‘Oh my goodness! What did Tesla do? What did they do?” he said. “It literally breaks every rule we tell to our students. It’s what we tell them not to do.”

Regardless, the Cybertruck started to infiltrate the cultural atmosphere. It was lampooned on The Simpsons. There were countless memes. It was embraced, very early, by rappers. Weeks after the unveiling, Travis Scott used his personal connections to the Tesla CEO (they did Christmas together with the Kardashian-Jenners) to snag a Cybertruck for his video for “Gang Gang,” a posse cut with the Cactus Jack crew.

Three years later, Pharrell Williams, 21 Savage, and Tyler, the Creator featured the Cybertruck in their video for “Cash In, Cash Out”—rendered in Claymation. Offset’s video for “Swing My Way” has Anok Yai sitting atop a Cybertruck. Bad Bunny said, “Me monté en la Cybertruck y me acordé de la Montero de los viejos tiempo.” Meek Mill said, “They was doing cyber attacks, so I bought a Cybertruck.”

The cars fascinated artists too. Julia Wachtel’s CyberChrist, on view at Todd Von Ammon’s DC gallery, von ammon co, earlier this year, pictures Jesus Christ pulling an elongated Cybertruck behind him. I recall with great happiness the perverse thrill of Frieda Toranzo Jaeger’s Cybertruck, a painting in her 2022 show at MoMA PS1. These artists were certainly taking a critical eye toward the Cybertruck, but for some art collectors, there was nothing ironic about it. At least, a specific kind of collector. When I arrived at the convention center for Art Basel Miami Beach in 2024, the first full year of Cybertruck distribution, there was a line of Cybertrucks wrapped around the block.

But that’s the thing about the Cybertruck: There was always more supply than demand. Musk initially hoped to sell 250,000 units per year. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, Tesla moved nearly 39,000 of them in 2024, a decent start. In 2025, sales dropped, then dropped again in 2026.

Perhaps the Cybertruck could have endured the ridicule of design experts, car enthusiasts, and aesthetes with even just a whiff of good taste if it weren’t for the massive backlash that accompanied Musk’s move into radical right-wing politics, and his full-throated support of Donald Trump. After his efforts at DOGE resulted in the gutting of USAID and other agencies, along with unprecedented and remorseless mass firings, Cybertrucks started getting vandalized around the country. Some owners tried to protect their weird boxy investments with mea culpa stickers—“I bought this before Elon went crazy,” etc.—but no one believed that, or really cared. The cars got defaced. No one stepped in to intervene. The Cybertrucks deserved it.

There was also a bleaker incident that parallels the Cybertruck at the Beverly Hills Hotel: the dystopian hellscape of the Cybertruck that exploded on the Las Vegas Strip, in front of the Trump International Hotel & Casino. The man responsible for that explosion served in the US Army, and authorities believe he suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound just before the vehicle detonated. The Beverly Hills crash was an accident in which no one was harmed—but the charred, deadly remains of the truck in Las Vegas seemed downright terrifying, a vision of American capitalism and greed that had met its grisly moment.

Perhaps now, with a new era of Washington poised to define the final years of this most delirious of decades, we’ll eventually look back at the Cybertruck with at least some nostalgia for its silliness, its boxy stupidity, its pop culture ubiquity. If it does linger in the annals of history, maybe we’ll think of the Cybertruck as a roadbound folly of the world’s first trillionaire, and a footnote in Musk’s legacy, for better or for worse.

Put it this way: By the time Hollywood studio heads arrived at the Polo Lounge for their Monday power lunches, the mess of the Cybertruck that had crashed at the Beverly Hills Hotel the night before was gone. Almost as if it never happened at all.
